# BZ-Age — Draft-07 Narration (v0.7.4)

# Series Cold Open / Prologue

About twenty-four hundred years ago, a Greek army was trying to walk home from Iraq.

The year was 401 BCE. Put that in the world of classical Greece, the Greece of Athens and Sparta. Socrates is still alive. The famous stand of the Spartans at Thermopylae happened about eighty years earlier. We are already thousands of years after the first cities, but still more than four centuries before the beginning of the calendar we use today.

One of the soldiers was an Athenian named Xenophon, a former student of Socrates. He and about ten thousand other Greeks had hired on with a prince of Persia. Persia was the great empire of the day. Its home was in what is now Iran, and it ruled everything from Turkey to the borders of India. The prince wanted his brother's throne, and he had marched his hired Greeks a thousand miles inland to take it.

It went badly. The prince was killed in the battle. Then the Greek commanders were invited to a meeting with the Persians, seized, and executed. So here were ten thousand men in the middle of somebody else's empire, with no employer and no generals, heading north along the Tigris River and hoping to reach the sea.

Xenophon lived, and years later he wrote the whole march down. That's how we know what he saw on the way.

This was river country, with fields and villages. Among them the army passed the remains of a much larger place, a city Xenophon calls deserted.

He describes a wall of clay brick on a stone base. He puts it at a hundred feet high and twenty-five feet thick. A hundred feet is roughly a ten-story building. Those are his reported dimensions, not a modern survey, but the impression is unmistakable: an enormous amount of building still stood above him. Nearby was a tall stone structure he calls a pyramid. People from the surrounding villages had climbed onto it to get away from the passing army.

What would the ruined city actually have looked like? We have to imagine some of that. Don't picture clean archaeological foundations with paths between them. Picture fallen brick gathering against the foot of a wall, its upper edges worn into irregular shapes. Where roofs had burned or fallen, rain could get into rooms that had once been protected. Mud brick can stand for centuries when it is maintained; left exposed, it gradually washes and crumbles back into earth. Stone footings can keep their outline after much of the building above them has gone.

And the wood? Some may have burned in the city's destruction. Useful beams and doors could have been carried away. Other timber could decay, while buried or charred fragments survived. A dry summer doesn't preserve an entire city like a sealed tomb. This landscape has wet seasons too. We can't reconstruct the condition of each house on the day Xenophon passed, but a standing wall did not mean that a habitable city remained behind it.

A day's march later the Greeks reached another deserted stronghold, larger than the first. Here Xenophon noticed shells in the dressed stone at the base of the wall.

Did he go inside? His account gives us no tour of the streets or houses. Nor does it name the people from whom he obtained the stories he records. We shouldn't turn that brief passage into an interview with the last inhabitants. We do know there were people living in the surrounding country; the villagers seeking shelter are right there in his account.

The stories are strange. The first city, he says, had belonged to the Medes, a people from the Iranian mountains. A Persian king had failed to take it until a cloud hid the sun and its defenders lost heart. The second city had a similar story, this time with thunder from Zeus. Xenophon recorded them and continued the march. He had an army to get home.

Scholars are fairly sure what he'd walked past. The first ruin was a city we call Nimrud. The second was Nineveh.

Nineveh had been a capital of Assyria, a kingdom centered on the Tigris River in what is now northern Iraq. Its kings conquered far beyond that homeland, reaching into Egypt. Nineveh became one of the great cities of the ancient world, a place of palaces, temples, and royal administration. The ruins belonged to a power that had once commanded much of the country through which these Greeks were struggling.

In 612 BCE its enemies sacked it. Its life as the capital of that empire was over.

That was two hundred and eleven years before Xenophon came by. From us, two hundred and eleven years takes you back to about 1815, the year of Waterloo. We know a good deal about Napoleon.

But look at the stories Xenophon records. They have Medes in them, and Persians, and a thunderstorm. They don't identify the Assyrian kings who had made these cities great. An educated Greek was passing the remains of an immense empire, and his account preserved a very incomplete explanation of what he saw.

That tells us something about the account, not everything about what people along the river remembered. Some knowledge and settlement survived the empire. What unsettles me is the gap: the masonry remained visible long after an accurate history of it had become difficult for this traveler to obtain.

And Assyria isn't even what this series is about.

Assyria was an heir. The cities, the writing, the law, the idea that one king could rule many peoples: all of that was ancient before Nineveh became an imperial capital. It came down from an older world, one that had already risen and fallen about eight hundred years before Xenophon's march.

We call that older world the Bronze Age. This series follows its development in the Near East and the eastern Mediterranean, from the growth of cities to an age of kings exchanging letters and ships carrying goods from distant countries. There were loans, contracts, customer complaints, and a peace treaty with an extradition clause. Around 1200 BCE, many of its kingdoms suffered profound disruption. Some cities burned, some governments disappeared, and some communities carried on. What survived, and what became difficult to remember, depended on where you stood.

So here's the question I'd like you to carry with you. How do people build a world that connected, live in it for centuries, and then lose so much of its working machinery? And why can one community keep its records while another eventually tells stories about the people who built the ruins?

Two things about how I'm going to tell it.

The first is the questions. I like simple ones. Why would anybody start farming? Why are the first cities on rivers? Why does an hour have sixty minutes? How do you mail a letter before there's paper? If iron is in every hillside, why did they bother with bronze? Most history skips those because the answers are supposed to be obvious. They aren't, and the real answers are usually better than the dates.

The second is the family.

Four thousand years is too long to follow any real person, and the Bronze Age has more kings with difficult names than anyone should have to remember. So I'm going to use a device, and I'm telling you now that it is one. We'll start in one house, with one household in it, and I'll point out five kinds of work that go on there. Someone works the field. Someone minds the stored grain. Someone is good at counting. Someone likes to walk to far places and come back with things. Someone is clever with tools.

In that first house those are just things people in one family do. As the world changes I'm going to follow each kind of work and see who's doing it. The minding of the grain will end up in the hands of kings. The counting will turn into writing. The walker becomes a merchant, the tool-maker becomes a smith, and the work in the field goes on for four thousand years and pays for everything else.

These aren't the same people, and they aren't one bloodline. They're a way of keeping track. But at almost every step there's a real person standing where one of them would stand, with a real name and sometimes real mail, and when that happens I'll say so.

Watch what happens to those five kinds of work. Some remain within a household. Others come to depend on people across a sea or beyond a range of mountains. Those connections make new kinds of wealth possible. They also create problems when the goods, payments, or protection people expect stop arriving. Following the work will help us see both the strength of that world and the different ways parts of it broke.

When the evidence runs out I'll tell you, once, and move on.

Now we go back. A long way.

Back past Xenophon and past Nineveh. Past the collapse, and past the first city. Back to about 5000 BCE, seven thousand years before you and me, and more than four and a half thousand years before that Greek army passed those walls.

Think about that gap for a second. From that house to Xenophon is nearly twice as far as from Xenophon to you.

We are before the great cities and written archives of this story. There's a small house that smells of smoke and sheep, and in it someone is about to wake up.


# Part 1 — Before Bronze

It's about 5000 BCE, seven thousand years ago. We're in a farming village in what is now northern Syria.

Your feet hurt.

That's the first thing every morning. It's still dark, there's a thin line of gray in the east, and you're awake because you never really got to sleep. You sleep on a mat on a dirt floor. Something always hurts. Your back, your hip, a tooth that's been wrong for weeks.

You're about thirty. To look at your hands, you'd guess fifty.

The house is one room. Mud-brick walls, a roof of timber and reeds black with smoke, and around a dozen smells that nobody seven thousand years from now would enjoy. It's your home, and it's a good one.

You live in a village of about sixty people, in the hill country of what is now northern Syria, a few days' walk inland from the Mediterranean. I should say that I've put this house together from what archaeologists have found in villages like it. Nobody dug up this particular family.

Six people sleep in this house when everyone's home, and between them they do five kinds of work that I'm going to follow.

There's you. You work the field. Barley mostly, some wheat, lentils, and you'll be bent over it from now until the light goes.

There's your grandmother, asleep by the back wall, next to the big clay bins. She's close to seventy, the oldest person in the village. She minds the grain. She knows how much there is, how much has to last until harvest, and who in the village owes this house a basket from last spring. Nobody opens a bin without her say.

There's your sister's boy, who is seven and does the sheep. He can't count past his fingers, so every morning he drops one pebble in a bag for each animal that goes out, and every evening he takes one pebble out for each animal that comes back. If there's a pebble left over, there's a sheep missing. He's hardly ever wrong. Your grandmother showed him the trick, and he took to it.

There's your brother, and he isn't here. Eleven days ago he walked north with two other men to get the black volcanic glass that makes the sharpest blades there are. He'll come back with a load of it and a head full of things he saw, and half of what he says nobody will believe.

And there's your cousin in the corner, already up, already chipping at a piece of flint. He's the one who makes the sickle blades, fixes the handles, and knows which rock breaks clean. He farms like everyone else. He's just better with his hands than you are.

And there's your sister, the boy's mother. She works the field beside you at harvest and does much of the work that keeps the household fed. Right now she's on her knees at the grinding stone, pushing one rock across another to turn grain into meal. Fine dust gathers around the stone. This is one long task in a day that also includes cooking and other work, not the only thing she ever does. She's the best baker in the village and she knows it. You've stopped hearing the scrape.

That's the household. A farmer, a keeper, a counter, a carrier, a maker. Right now those aren't jobs. They're what each person happens to be good at, and everyone eats from the same pot.

The first pyramid in Egypt is twenty-four centuries in the future, and the Greeks and Romans are further off than that.

Look at what isn't here.

There is no city in the world this household knows. The biggest crowd you've stood in might be a seasonal gathering of a few hundred people. Your familiar country is the land you can walk across and return from. Your brother has been further. Beyond that, you depend on other people's stories.

Nothing has ever been written down. Everything anybody knows is inside somebody's head, and when the old woman who knows the plants dies, whatever she didn't teach somebody dies too.

In this imagined village there is no palace collecting a regular share of the harvest. There are people others listen to. Your grandmother is one. A stronger village could raid you. Authority and inequality haven't waited for cities to appear, but the distant officials and written demands we will meet later are not part of this household's day.

Your tools are stone, bone and wood. The horse is a wild animal that you'd eat if you could catch one. Your cattle are one step removed from a wild ox that stands six feet at the shoulder and still lives in the woods past your fields. There are lions in the rough country, and the rough country is where you live.

And your food is missing half of what you'd expect. Bread, cheese, lentils, olives if you're lucky, honey for a treat. No tomatoes, no potatoes, no corn, no peppers. Those crops come from the Americas and will not enter this region's kitchens until thousands of years later. The old Mediterranean kitchen everybody imagines is sitting here with half its ingredients not yet arrived.

Everything I'm going to tell you for the next several hours grows out of this room. So before we follow those kinds of work into the cities, I want to look back at how people came to live this way. We'll visit a few earlier settlements, then return to this house.

About twelve thousand years ago, near the end of the last Ice Age, people in parts of southwest Asia were beginning the long transition toward farming. Hunting and gathering had sustained human communities for vastly longer. So why begin changing a way of getting food that already worked?

Hunger is one possible answer. More people, fewer animals to hunt, a changing climate: any of those could make a new food supply attractive. But farming began in different places under different conditions, and a simple story of starving people being forced to invent it leaves too much out.

In the 1960s an American crop scientist named Jack Harlan went to the hills of southeastern Turkey, where wild wheat still grows in thick stands the way it always has. He made himself a Stone Age sickle, a flint blade in a wooden handle, and he went out and harvested the wild stuff by hand and timed himself. He'd never done it before. He got about two pounds of clean grain an hour. He did the arithmetic and published it: a family working those hillsides for three weeks, at the right time of year, without killing themselves, could bring in more grain than they could eat in twelve months.

Three weeks of work for a year of food, from plants that nobody planted or watered.

That's only the cutting. It leaves out hauling it home, keeping it dry, and the hours of pounding and grinding before any of it is dinner. Ask your sister. But as a harvest it's astonishing.

Harlan's experiment doesn't tell us what every ancient household could harvest. It shows why we shouldn't picture all gatherers as people barely scratching a living from an empty landscape. Some wild resources were extraordinarily productive. That makes planting a crop something to explain, not an obvious improvement.

I'll give you three pieces of an answer. I think they're all true at once.

The first is bread. In the black desert of northeastern Jordan there's a fireplace that hunter-gatherers used about fourteen thousand years ago, and in the ashes archaeologists found burnt crumbs of flatbread. Somebody had gathered wild grain, pounded it, sieved it, mixed it with water and baked it. That's four thousand years before anyone in that region was farming. Bread is older than farming. People were going to a great deal of trouble over grain, long before grain was their living, apparently because they liked what you could make from it. Some archaeologists think they were brewing with it too. That one's argued, but I wouldn't bet against it.

The second piece is a hill.

In southeastern Turkey, in the same country Harlan walked, there's a place called Göbekli Tepe. It's a set of stone rings. Each ring is made of huge T-shaped limestone pillars, some eighteen feet tall and weighing ten tons or more, carved with foxes, vultures, scorpions, wild bulls and cranes. The carving is good. It was built around 9500 BCE.

The people who built it were hunter-gatherers. They had no farms, no pottery, no metal and no draft animals. They cut ten-ton pillars out of bedrock with stone tools, dragged them, stood them upright and decorated them, about a thousand years before there's any sign of farmed crops around there. They may have been tending the wild stands. We can't tell. A thousand years is further than from us back to the Norman conquest of England.

That's the wrong order. Every textbook model says you get farming first, then surplus, then spare time, then monuments. Temples are supposed to come after granaries. A German archaeologist named Klaus Schmidt walked up that hill in 1994. An earlier survey had written it off as a medieval cemetery. He looked at the carved stone poking out of the plowed soil and knew within the hour it was something else. He dug there for twenty years, until he died, and he summed it up in one line: first came the temple, then the city.

The slogan is a little too clean. Since he died, diggers have found signs that people lived at the site, not just visited, and they've found a whole cluster of sister sites in the same hills. So it's less one impossible temple than an impossible neighborhood. But the core stands. The stones are older than the farms.

What was it for? Nobody knows, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who tells you. But I'll tell you what they found on the site besides pillars: thousands of grinding stones, and stone vats big enough to hold forty gallons. Whatever else was happening on that hill, people were processing wild grain there in bulk. Somebody was feeding a crowd.

Here's what I think happened, and it's a guess. You can't raise a ten-ton pillar with your cousins. You need a crowd, and you have to feed it while it works, and the best way to get a crowd to show up and haul stone is to throw a feast. Bread, meat, and probably something to drink. To do that every year you need a lot of grain in one place at one time. So you start managing the wild stands. You come back to the same hillsides. You guard them. You keep some seed back.

On that reading, people didn't settle down and then build temples. They wanted the gathering, the gathering needed feeding, and the feeding turned them into farmers.

The third piece is the one that matters most for everything that follows, and it's very plain. Grain keeps.

Meat rots in days. Fruit rots in a week. Dry grain in a sealed bin is good for years. And the moment a family has a year of food in a clay bin at the back of the house, three things have happened to them that they didn't decide. They've stopped moving, because you don't walk away from a year of food. They have something that can be measured, by the basket, which means it can be owed. And they have something that can be taken.

People had stored food and valued possessions before farming. Grain adds a particularly useful kind of reserve: a pile that can be counted, divided, lent, and taken. In some places, stores like these will become part of much larger institutions. It takes a very long time, and a bin does not turn into a kingdom by itself.

Now the bad news, and this is where I part company with the cheerful version of this story.

In many places, the transition to farming came with serious costs. Skeletal studies often find poorer childhood nutrition, dental disease, and heavy repetitive work. The pattern varies between communities, and a worn joint doesn't identify a person's exact daily chore. But think again about the work before breakfast in our house: grain has to become food, one batch at a time. A successful harvest can still demand an exhausting life.

They were sicker too. A hunter-gatherer camp moves on from its own filth. A village sits in it. People, cattle, pigs, sheep, goats and dogs sharing a water supply, year after year. The political scientist James Scott called the early farming village a "multispecies resettlement camp", and a lot of the diseases that have troubled us ever since came out of that arrangement.

It wasn't the same everywhere. In some regions people kept their height and their health. But the costs turn up too often to wave away.

So why did it spread? Because it didn't need anyone's approval. A band of foragers has to carry everything they own, including their toddlers, so they space their children years apart. A village with stored food, and porridge to wean a baby onto, can raise its children closer together. Over generations, a settled population can grow faster than its neighbors. That can help farming spread without making it a healthier life for each person. But foraging does not disappear everywhere, and people can combine the two ways of getting food.

In a valley supporting a dense farming population, returning entirely to hunting and gathering can become much harder. There may be too many mouths for the land to feed that way. The door gets harder to open.

For many communities, I think farming could become a trap. I don't mean anyone set it. Nobody chose the whole of it, and nobody alive at the time could have seen the shape of it. Each family made a sensible decision about next winter, and generations of sensible decisions could make people dependent on a demanding way of life. Much later, some farming societies supported cities and writing. Those later possibilities didn't make the work any easier for the people at our grinding stone.

Keep that pattern in your pocket. A long run of sensible choices that walks people into something nobody would have signed up for. We'll see it again, on a bigger scale.

Now move forward through those earlier settlements, still on our way back to the house we began in.

By 8000 BCE there's a settlement at Jericho, by a spring in the Jordan Valley, with two or three thousand people in it. They built a stone wall around it, and against the inside of the wall they built a round stone tower twenty-eight feet high with a staircase up the middle. Nobody knows what the tower was for. What it tells me is that somebody could already get a lot of people to haul rock for a purpose that wasn't dinner. Thousands of years later the Bible would set a story at Jericho about walls falling down. That story is about a much later town on the same spot. This first wall was older than its tellers could have imagined.

By 7000 BCE there's something stranger in central Turkey. It's called Çatalhöyük, and several thousand people lived there for well over a thousand years. It had no streets. None. The houses were built wall to wall like cells in a honeycomb, and you got into yours through a hole in the roof. To go anywhere you walked across your neighbors' ceilings.

Inside, the floors were replastered so many times that archaeologists count the layers like tree rings. And under those floors were the dead. People at Çatalhöyük buried their dead beneath the platforms they slept on. Sometimes they dug a skull back up later, plastered a face onto it, painted it, and kept it in the house. The dead weren't in a cemetery on the edge of town. They were under the bed. And DNA from those bones has a surprise in it. In the town's later centuries, many of the people buried under the same floor weren't related to each other at all. Whatever a household was in that town, it was more than a family.

We can't recover exactly what those people believed. But picture the practical business of that town: someone crossing a roof with a load, a ladder leading down into a room, a hearth needing fuel, grain needing grinding. The dead beneath the floor belonged to a space in which the living were still cooking, working, and sleeping.

Which brings us back to our imagined household around 5000 BCE. Five people are at home; the brother who trades is away. Now the bins and the grinding stone have a history behind them. They are part of how this family makes it through the year.

And in the corner, your cousin has put down the flint. He's holding something green.

Here's the second simple question. How does anybody figure out that metal comes from rock? Because it isn't obvious. Copper ore doesn't look like copper. It looks like a crumbly green or blue stone.

People had known copper itself for a long time. Now and then you find it lying around as pure metal, in little nuggets, and for three thousand years before your morning people had been hammering those into beads and pins. It's metalworking of a kind, but it treats the nugget like a very soft rock.

The leap is discovering that heating some of those green minerals with charcoal can release copper. It isn't just a matter of melting a rock. The fuel helps remove oxygen bound to the copper in the mineral. The heat, the ore, and the air reaching the fire all matter. Getting useful metal out repeatedly takes control of those conditions. How someone first stumbled on it, nobody knows. My guess is a potter. Potters already had kilns that ran hot, and they were already using ground-up green stone as a pigment. Sooner or later someone opened a kiln and found a bright bead of metal where the paint had been.

The oldest solid evidence of people doing it on purpose is from about 5000 BCE, right around your morning, at a village in what is now Serbia, twelve hundred miles northwest of your house. Within a few centuries it turns up in Iran and Turkey as well.

And it changes your cousin's life more than anybody's. Smelting takes days, and a great deal of fuel, and years of getting it wrong. At first he does it in the slack season and farms the rest of the year. But the better he gets, the more people want what he makes, and the more of his dinner comes from them.

Over generations, some people doing the Maker's work will be able to make it their main livelihood. We aren't following this cousin's descendants.

Your brother's life changes too. Copper ore sits where it sits. Most valleys have none. If yours doesn't, somebody has to walk to a valley that does and bring it back, and he's already the one who walks.

One side trip before we go on, because it sets up a puzzle I'm going to leave you with.

On the far side of the world, around Lake Superior, there's more pure natural copper than almost anywhere on Earth. Lumps of it in streambeds. And around nine thousand years ago the people living there started working it. They hammered it, heated it, shaped it into knives and spear points and fishhooks. Thousands of those tools survive. Those hunters and fishers were among the first metalworkers anywhere, and nobody taught them.

Then, after several thousand years, they mostly stopped. The knives and points went back to stone. Copper became beads and ornaments. And the reason seems to be thoroughly practical. People have tested it: a fresh stone edge cuts about as well as a copper one, and it's far less work to make. They had metal, they compared it with what they had, and it lost.

So here's the puzzle. Those people had metal before almost anyone. They had lakes and rivers running everywhere, which is the best transport there is. They had fish and game in quantities the Near East would have envied. And no city ever rose there. No kings, no writing, for thousands of years.

Why not? What did southern Iraq have that Lake Superior didn't? I'll answer it next time. I'll only say that it isn't the copper, and that the answer is sitting at the back wall of your house, next to your grandmother.

Back to the cousin, because there's a cost here too.

Pure copper is soft. A copper axe bends. What you want is something harder, and the first way anyone found to get it was by accident. A lot of copper ores have another element mixed in, and when you smelt those ores, the metal that comes out is harder, casts more cleanly and keeps an edge. The smiths didn't know why. They just learned which rocks gave the good metal and went looking for more of them.

The other element is arsenic.

Smelting it puts arsenic in the smoke. Breathe that smoke for years and it damages the nerves in your hands and feet. You get weak. You get clumsy. You start to limp.

There's an old idea that this is why the Greek god of the forge, Hephaestus, is lame. He's the only Olympian with a damaged body, and he's the smith. I can't prove the connection and neither can anyone else. But I like it as a possibility: that the one thing the first metalworkers left behind about themselves is a god who walks the way they did.

So picture your cousin a few years from now. He has the best diet in the village, because people bring him food. He has a kind of respect no farmer gets. He makes the axe that the headman carries on feast days. And his hands are going numb, and he has no idea why.

A better recipe is coming. Later smiths will find that a little of a different metal, tin, does the same job as arsenic and doesn't cripple you. Nine parts copper and one part tin makes bronze, the real thing, the metal the age is named for. But tin is rare. It's found in a handful of places, all of them far from anywhere these people live. Getting it will become a problem for people doing the Carrier's work, linking distant communities through trade.

Third question, and then I'll let you go. Who was the first person to own something?

You can't dig that person up. Owning doesn't leave a mark in the ground. But you can dig up the first people who owned so much that it had to be buried with them.

In 1972, in the city of Varna on the Black Sea coast of Bulgaria, a man running a digger was cutting a trench for a cable and noticed bits of yellow metal in his bucket. He had hit a cemetery from about 4500 BCE. It's the same part of the world where we just saw the first smelting, a few centuries later.

The cemetery held around three hundred graves. Most had little in them: a pot, a flint blade. A handful were rich. The richest, which archaeologists call Grave 43, held a man in his forties or fifties with nearly a thousand gold objects on and around his body. Bracelets, beads, discs sewn to his clothes, a gold-handled axe that had never cut anything. About three pounds of gold in all, the oldest worked gold ever found anywhere.

Think about what had to be true for that grave to exist. Someone mined that gold. Someone worked it, every bead, by hand. Many people spent a very long time making things that one man got to wear, and when he died the village put all of it in the ground with him, where nobody could use it, to make a point about who he had been. And most of his neighbors went into the same hillside with a pot.

This isn't your family, and it's a long way from your village. But it's the earliest place we can see the end of the single pot. On your morning everybody in the house ate the same dinner. Five hundred years later, on the Black Sea, one man is buried in gold and most people aren't.

Now run the clock forward, quickly, because nothing in the next stretch looks like an event.

From your morning to the year 3200 BCE is eighteen hundred years. About seventy generations. Changes accumulate at different speeds in different places: a settlement grows, a store expands, more people depend on work done outside their own house.

But the five kinds of work are changing. We aren't following this household's descendants through eighteen hundred years. We're following people who do the same kinds of work.

Minding grain can become more than a household chore. Where larger stores support a community, the person controlling them has a say in who eats in a bad year. Our Keeper now stands for that kind of authority, not for your grandmother's heir.

Other people count what comes into the stores. Among their tools are little shaped pieces of clay, a cone for a measure of grain, a ball for a bigger one, and they're kept in the storehouse as a record of who brought what. The Counter works for the Keeper.

Some Makers can spend more of their time making things, supplied with food by other people.

Carriers travel farther, on foot, with pack animals, and in boats. More goods can move between communities.

And the Farmer? Still in the field. The plow has arrived, pulled by an ox, so one man can now work far more ground. That sounds like good news for you. It mostly means there's more grain to hand over to the man who holds the store.

And the story moves. The place where all of this first comes together isn't the hill country. It's eight hundred miles to the southeast, on the flat plain where the two great rivers of Iraq run down to the sea. By 3200 BCE the biggest settlement on that plain isn't a village anymore. It's something that has never existed before.

It's going to be loud.


# Part 2 — The First Cities

Before we go anywhere, look at a clock.

Sixty seconds in a minute. Sixty minutes in an hour. Nobody alive chose that. It's an odd number to build time on, and by the end of this part you'll know who to blame.

It's 3200 BCE. Eighteen hundred years have gone by since the morning in the one-room house, about as long as from the Roman Empire at its height to today. And we've moved, eight hundred miles to the southeast, out of the hills and down onto the flat plain at the bottom of Iraq, where two rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates, run side by side to the Persian Gulf.

The people we'll follow here aren't the family from the first house. They're the people doing the same five kinds of work, in a very different place. And I want to start by asking why anyone lives here at all, because on paper it's a terrible spot.

Rainfall on the southern plain is too low for dependable farming without river water. There is little local building stone, no convenient supply of long construction timbers, and no local metal ore. But the mud and reeds are useful materials, not merely things the villagers are stuck with. You can make walls, roofs, boats, containers, and eventually writing surfaces from what this landscape provides.

What it has is mud. Every spring the snow melts in the mountains of Turkey, and the two rivers come down carrying the mountains with them, ground to powder. Where the land flattens out, the water slows and drops what it's carrying. Southern Iraq is that mud, laid down a flood at a time for thousands of years. It's some of the richest soil on the planet. Put a seed in it and you get back several times what the hills ever gave.

There's a catch that helps explain the work a settlement needs to organize. The flood comes in spring, which is exactly when the barley is ripe and standing in the field. In the autumn, when you need water to plant, the rivers are low. The water arrives at the wrong time of year, every year. So to farm there at all you have to move it. Dig a channel from the river, hold the water back, let it out when you want it. A village can manage a small ditch among its own people. But the ditches join up, and the bigger the network gets, the more somebody has to settle who digs, who gets the water first, and who clears out the silt.

Somebody has to settle those arguments. That doesn't tell us by itself whether the answer is a council, a powerful household, a temple, or a king. Irrigation creates a practical problem of cooperation; it isn't a machine that automatically produces one kind of government.

So here's the first simple question. Why are the first big cities of the ancient world on rivers? Iraq on the Tigris and Euphrates, Egypt on the Nile, India on the Indus, China on the Yellow River.

Water for the fields is part of it. Transport is another part. A loaded donkey can carry roughly a hundred and fifty pounds, depending on the animal and the journey. The animals and their handlers also need food and water, and a long trip costs time and labor. Boats can move much heavier loads with fewer people. Downstream the current helps; upstream a boat may need towing, paddling, or a favorable wind. River transport isn't effortless, but it changes what is practical to bring into a city.

A large city needs food arriving day after day, much of it grown beyond the houses its inhabitants can see. Waterways made that easier in southern Iraq. They are an important advantage here, not a rule that explains the location of every early city.

Let's follow an imagined load of barley. The route and the people are a way into the work; they are not a surviving account of one particular delivery.

It starts with the Farmer. He's in a field a day's walk from the river, and it's harvest. Notice what's in his hand. It's a sickle made of baked clay. There's no stone down here for a blade and metal is far too precious for a farmhand, so they fire a curved piece of mud until it's hard as pottery and sharpen the edge. It breaks constantly. Archaeologists find broken clay sickles all over southern Iraq, in the thousands.

He cuts the barley, threshes it, and measures it into baskets. And then a share of those baskets leaves. It isn't his. The canal that waters this field was dug on somebody's orders and it's maintained on somebody's orders, and that somebody takes a cut of everything the canal makes possible. Part of what the Farmer grew goes onto a barge.

The barge goes down a side channel to the river, and from there it has to be hauled to the city against the current. That's the Carrier's job. In the first house, the man who did his kind of work walked to the mountains for volcanic glass. This one walks a towpath with a rope over his shoulder, hauling other people's grain. He's never seen a city. In two days he will.

You see it long before you get there. The land is flat as a table, so anything tall shows for miles, and what shows is a white building on top of a man-made hill. It's been coated in plaster made from gypsum so it catches the sun. A farmer half a day away can look up from his work and see the god's house shining.

The city is called Uruk. Around 3200 BCE somewhere between twenty-five and fifty thousand people live in it. Nobody knows the number more closely than that, and it doesn't matter, because either figure makes it an extraordinary concentration of people for its time. It covers about a square mile.

Picture the Carrier arriving from a small village. He passes animals, cooking fires, workshops, loads being carried toward the water. Smoke and river mud are familiar smells; the number of people is not. The layout is harder to take in than a village where every path leads to someone he knows. A city is a new problem for his eyes before it becomes an idea in his head.

And he's surrounded by strangers. In his village every face comes with a name and a family and probably a grudge. Here he can walk for an hour and not recognize one person. I think places like this are where human beings first found out what it is to be anonymous. I've never been able to decide whether that's freedom or loneliness, and I don't think the people who first felt it knew either.

He pulls the barge to the quay. A man is waiting with a small slab of wet clay in his hand.

That man is the Counter, and we'll get to what he's holding. First, where does the grain go?

It goes to the biggest institution in the city, and I have to be careful how I describe it, because we don't have a word for it.

It's a temple. It belongs to a goddess named Inanna, who is the goddess of love and of war and of the evening star, and it's called the House of Heaven. But if you walked in you wouldn't think church. You'd think warehouse, and factory, and payroll office. There are storerooms full of barley. There are weaving sheds, breweries, bakeries, potteries and a metal shop. A great many people work there, and they're fed out of those storerooms.

Your grandmother's grain bins, the ones at the back of the house in Part 1, have turned into this.

I like to call it a granary with a god on top, and I'll stand by that as long as you hear the second half as loudly as the first. The people who worked there weren't cynics. They believed, completely, that the goddess lived in that building. She was present in her statue. In later centuries we have the routine written down: she was served two meals a day, dressed, and put to bed. The whole operation was her household and everyone in it was her staff.

A caution. Scholars used to say the temple owned everything in these early cities, every field and every worker. That idea came from one archive in one city, and it's been walked back. There were families with their own land, and there was private dealing. But the temple was the biggest player by a long way, and it's the one that kept records.

And now I owe you an answer. Last time I left a question on the shore of Lake Superior. The people there had copper before almost anyone, more waterways than Iraq, plenty to eat, and never built a city. Why not?

Look at what Uruk is made of. It isn't copper. Uruk has hardly any metal. It's made of barley. The storerooms hold it, the workers are paid in it, the records count it, and the wall exists to protect it.

Grain is a peculiar food. It ripens all at once, in an open field, where anyone can see how much you've got. It can be divided down to a cupful and piled up by the ton. And it keeps for years. The political scientist James Scott listed its properties: grain is, in his words, "visible, divisible, assessable, storable, transportable, and rationable." In plain English, grain is the food you can tax.

Now look at what Lake Superior offered. Fish. Deer. Wild rice, growing in a thousand scattered marshes. You can live very well on that, probably better than a farmer in Iraq. And you can keep it. People around the Great Lakes dried fish and put up wild rice for the winter. What's hard is for somebody else to collect it. There's no field to inspect, and no harvest week when the whole crop is standing in the open waiting to be counted. A family's food is spread across a lake country, and it's theirs.

So here's one part of my answer. Copper alone doesn't make a city. Large populations need food supplies and ways of organizing work beyond a single household. Stored grain made that possible in particular ways at Uruk. It does not follow that every society without an Uruk lacked the resources, intelligence, or institutions to build one.

There's a second case that points the same way. One crop that became particularly important to large settlements in North America was corn, and corn came from Mexico. It took thousands of years to adapt to northern summers. Around a thousand years ago it finally took hold in the Mississippi valley, and within about a century there was a city across the river from where St. Louis is now. It's called Cahokia. Ten or twenty thousand people, about the size of London at the time, and an earth pyramid with a bigger footprint than the Great Pyramid in Egypt. People who had no contact with the Old World got a grain they could grow in bulk, and within a few generations they had a city. Corn wasn't the only reason. I don't think the timing is an accident, though.

Back to the quay.

Second question. What do you buy things with, before there's money?

There are no coins. There won't be for another twenty-five hundred years. For big deals people weigh out silver on a balance, but a barge-puller might go a season without touching silver. What he gets is issued to him.

Archaeologists digging in Uruk and every town connected with it find one object more than any other. It's a rough little bowl, about the size of your two cupped hands, with a slanted rim. It's ugly. It was made by pressing clay into a mold, fast, with no care at all, and it was thrown away after use. They turn up by the hundred thousand. Whole rooms are full of them.

The leading explanation is that it's a ration bowl. You line up, you get it filled with barley or bread or porridge, and that's your pay for the day. Not everyone agrees, and the bowls were probably used for more than one thing. But I think of it as a disposable cup from the company cafeteria, turned out by the hundred thousand, five thousand years ago.

You got beer as well. Beer was food here. It was thick and cloudy and you drank it through a reed straw to keep the husks out of your teeth, and everybody drank it, from the man on the towpath to whoever sat at the top of the temple.

And notice something odd. In a hundred and fifty years of digging, nobody has found a marketplace in one of these early cities, no square built for buying and selling. People certainly traded, at a doorway or at the city gate or on the quay. But for a lot of people in Uruk, the middle of the economy was a line you stood in.

So who's in the line?

Weavers, among others, and most of the weavers are women. Cloth is what this plain has to sell. It has no stone, timber or metal, so it sells wool, and in the centuries to come the weaving sheds of these cities will employ thousands.

This is where the Farmer's sister's kind of work has gone. In the first house she ground the grain and baked the bread and was proud of it. Here the grinding and the weaving are done in rows, for an institution, and counted. And here I have to tell you something plainly, and I'll only say it at length this once.

Some of the women in that shed came because they were hungry and the temple fed people who worked. Some were widows and orphans the institution had taken in. And some were owned. The records list people handed over to pay off a family's debt, and people captured in raids on other towns and brought back. And the records mostly don't bother to tell those groups apart. Walked in or dragged in, a woman appears the same way: a number of workers, and a number of bowls.

Slavery isn't a late corruption of civilization. It's there in the first city, in the first records, written with the same marks that count the sheep. I'll point to it again as we go. I won't soften it.

Now. The man on the quay with the wet clay.

Third question. Why does a city need writing? You'd think writing was invented to record stories, or prayers, or the deeds of kings. It wasn't, and the true answer is better.

Remember the boy with the pebbles, one for each sheep. By now his line keeps the storehouse records with little clay tokens. A cone means a small measure of grain. A ball means a big one. A cylinder is an animal. If a farmer owes the temple five measures, you set five cones aside for him.

That works in a village. It doesn't work when you're shipping grain between people who've never met. How does the man on the quay know the barge-puller didn't help himself to a basket on the way?

So someone came up with a seal. You take the tokens for the shipment and close them up inside a hollow ball of wet clay, about the size of a tennis ball, and you send that along with the barge. At the other end, they crack it open and count. The tokens inside have to match the grain on board. It's a tamper-proof packing slip.

It has one flaw. To check it you have to break it. So someone had the idea of pressing the tokens into the outside of the wet ball before sealing them inside. Now you can read the contents off the surface.

And then somebody, and I'd love to know who, noticed that if the marks are on the outside, you don't need anything on the inside. You don't need the ball at all. Flatten the clay into a little pillow, press the marks into it, and you're finished.

That's a tablet. And in this part of the world it's the beginning of writing: a packing slip with the packing removed.

A scholar named Denise Schmandt-Besserat pieced that sequence together starting in the 1970s. The part about numbers is solid. The earliest number signs really are pictures of those tokens. How many of the other signs came from tokens is argued, and some plainly came from elsewhere, from the pictures on seals for one. But as an account of how counting turned into marks on clay, I think it holds.

For the first several centuries, that is all writing did. The oldest tablets on Earth come from the trash heaps of Inanna's temple, about five thousand of them, and there isn't a story or a prayer in the lot. They're barley, sheep, cloth, beer, and lists of job titles. Writing couldn't yet record a sentence. It could record "five sheep" and whose they were.

Much of the later writing from these southern cities records a language called Sumerian. Keep that name: the script will go on to serve other languages too.

It took generations for anyone to realize the marks could stand for sounds, not just things. Draw an arrow, and you mean an arrow. But in Sumerian the word for arrow sounded like the word for life. So draw an arrow and mean life. Once you make that jump you can spell anything a person can say: names, verbs, promises, lies, poems.

One tablet from this period records an enormous delivery of barley over thirty-seven months, and at the end there are two signs that seem to be a signature: Kushim. It may be a person's name. It may be the title of an office. Nobody's sure. But if it's a name, then the first human being whose name we know wasn't a king, or a priest, or a hero. He was an accountant, and what we know about him is that he was responsible for the barley.

I find that completely fitting. The oldest writing tradition on Earth, the one that will go on to produce the first laws and the first letters and the first poem with an author's name on it, began with somebody trying to keep track of grain.

And the Counter isn't a boy with a bag of pebbles anymore. He's a specialist with a skill nobody else has.

That skill has to be taught, and it's hard. The system ends up with hundreds of signs. So they opened schools. The word for it meant "the tablet house."

I'm going to jump ahead fourteen hundred years for a minute, because that's where the best evidence is. We have their homework. Thousands of practice tablets survive from around 1800 BCE, when the system had been running for about as long as the English language has existed. The teacher writes a line on the top half, the pupil copies it underneath, and you can see the kid's wobbly version next to the neat one. Some have doodles on the back. One has a child's tooth marks in it. And we have the students' own essays about school, which are mostly complaints about being beaten: for bad handwriting, for talking, for standing up without permission.

Along with the signs, they learned arithmetic. And this is the clock.

These people counted in sixties. I can't tell you why for certain and neither can anyone else. The best guess is practical. Sixty divides evenly by two, three, four, five and six, which is a wonderful thing if you spend your day splitting rations and fields and inheritances and you don't have decimals. Whatever the reason, their arithmetic ran on sixty. A thousand years later the astronomers of Babylon, who inherited it, used it to divide the circle of the sky. The Greeks took the Babylonian tables because they worked. The Arab astronomers kept them. And when medieval scholars put them into Latin, they called the first small division of the hour the "minute part," and the second small division the "second."

So the sixty on your wrist is five thousand years old. Nobody in Uruk had minutes or seconds. They had the arithmetic, and the rest of us inherited it. The twenty-four hours come from Egypt, which is a different story. Your watch is a joint project between two civilizations that never knew they were collaborating.

Back to Uruk around 3200 BCE, and the quay, before those later schoolrooms. That's the journey: field, barge, storehouse, bowl, tablet, school. Most of what makes a city is somewhere on that path.

Now the hard question. Why would anyone put up with it?

Think about what's being asked of the Farmer. He hands over part of his crop to people he's never met. He's called up to dig canals. His sister is in a weaving shed. Why does he agree?

Some of it is plain: the canal is real, and without it there's no crop. Some of it is force. And some of it, I think, is that he believed in it. We can't ask him. But there's an object that shows what he was told.

It's a stone vase about three feet tall, carved in Uruk around 3200 BCE, and it's covered in pictures arranged in bands. Read it from the bottom. First, wavy lines: water. Above that, barley and date palms. Above that, sheep. Above that, a line of men, naked, carrying baskets and jars. And at the top, a figure presenting all of it to a woman standing at a gate. That's Inanna, or her priestess.

It's a diagram of the whole system, drawn by the people who ran it. Water makes grain, grain makes sheep, men carry it up, and it's given to the goddess. Everything flows upward to her house. And in return she makes the water come again next year.

Their stories said the same thing. In the version we have, written down later, the gods originally did their own farming and got sick of it, so they made human beings out of clay to do the work. People exist to feed the gods. The temple isn't taking your barley. It's collecting what you were created to give.

And who stands between the people and the goddess, handing her the offering? On the vase, there's a man in a long skirt at the front of the line. He turns up in other carvings from Uruk too, feeding the temple flocks, leading prisoners. He's the head of the goddess's household.

That's the Keeper. The one who minded the grain bins is now the steward of a goddess, and when the city fights its neighbors over water, he's the one who leads. In later centuries his title will be a word that means "big man", and we translate it as king. Later hymns even describe a ceremony each new year in which the king plays the goddess's husband. Scholars argue about how literally that was acted out. What matters is the claim: he rules because she chose him.

So why did anyone agree to have a king? Because by the time there was one, he wasn't asking for himself.

Move forward about six hundred years, to around 2600 BCE, and you can see how far that had gone.

About forty miles downriver from Uruk is a different city with a confusingly similar name. Uruk, and Ur. We'll be back at Ur more than once. In the 1920s an English archaeologist named Leonard Woolley dug its cemetery, and among two thousand ordinary graves he found sixteen that weren't ordinary.

In one lay a woman whose seal gives her name, Puabi. She was wearing a headdress of gold leaves and gold ribbons, with beads of deep blue stone from Afghanistan, fifteen hundred miles away. In another tomb there was a wooden harp with a bull's head on the front in gold, with a blue stone beard. There was a board game, twenty squares inlaid with shell, with its dice. People kept playing that game for the next two thousand years. A later tablet explains the rules, and a curator at the British Museum has worked out a playable version. I love that these people took their music and their board games into the grave with them.

And then there's the pit.

In one spot, with no tomb chamber beside it at all, Woolley found seventy-four bodies laid out in rows. Six were men with weapons. Sixty-eight were women, in gold and silver ribbons, some still holding harps. Who they were buried to accompany, we don't know.

Woolley thought they'd walked down the ramp, drunk poison from a cup, and lain down to die quietly. It's a peaceful picture, and for eighty years it was the story. A few years ago researchers put two skulls from this cemetery through a CT scanner: a woman's from that pit, and a soldier's from one of the tombs. Both had been punched through with a pointed weapon. There were signs the bodies had been heated and treated to preserve them and then arranged.

Two skulls can't tell us how the other seventy-odd died, or how many went willingly. I doubt it was all of them.

That's what the Keeper's line had become, six hundred years after the vase. Someone who could take seventy-four people into the grave.

We don't know the name of anyone in that pit. We know hardly any names from Uruk at all, apart from a clerk or two. The city counted its people. Mostly it didn't remember them.

One name got out a different way, as a story, and how that happened tells you something. Step back about a century from those graves. Later tradition places a king called Gilgamesh at Uruk around 2700 BCE. He was probably real. Later tradition says he built the city wall, which ran six miles around.

That's everything we know. What we have instead is the Epic of Gilgamesh, a poem that grew over the next fifteen hundred years. In it he's two-thirds god, he wrestles a wild man who becomes his best friend, the friend dies, and Gilgamesh goes to the end of the world looking for a way not to die. He doesn't find one. He comes home and looks at the wall. The poem opens and closes by telling you to do the same: climb up on it, look at the brickwork.

It's one of the best things anyone has ever written, and it has almost nothing to do with the man. Somewhere back there, probably, was a real king, and a story grew over him until the story was all that was left.

Watch for that. It happens to everyone in this series who gets remembered at all. It's going to happen, in the end, to the whole Bronze Age.

Let me pull back before we finish, and return to around 3000 BCE. We've followed Uruk, with a visit to its neighbor Ur, but those cities weren't the whole world.

Around 3000 BCE only a tiny share of humanity lived in a city. Everybody else was a farmer or a herder or a hunter who had never heard of Uruk. What we've been looking at is a tiny, bright exception.

It wasn't the only one. In Egypt, around 3100 BCE, a king joined the whole Nile valley into one country. Egypt's river was kinder than Iraq's. It flooded at the right time of year, and it flows north while the wind blows south, so you can drift one way and sail back the other. It's a two-way highway. Egypt had its own rival towns for a time. But early on, one king took the whole valley, and after that it mostly stayed one country. And the Egyptians went a step further than Uruk about who that king was. He wasn't the god's steward. He was a god.

And further east, a few centuries later, on the Indus River in what's now Pakistan, a third civilization would build cities with something Uruk never had: a plan. Straight streets on a grid. Bricks all the same size. Covered drains. And as far as anyone can find, no palaces and no giant temples. They had writing too, on little stone seals. Nobody has ever been able to read it. Hold onto that. It's the last thing we'll talk about in this series.

These places already knew of each other, faintly. That blue stone in Puabi's headdress came from one valley in Afghanistan. It reached Iraq, and it reached Egypt, passed from hand to hand by people who each knew the next stop and nothing beyond it. Nobody ran that chain. Nobody could see all of it. And already the cities couldn't do without it. They had mud and barley and wool. Everything else had to come from far away through people they'd never meet.

So where's the family?

They don't live in the same house anymore. They don't eat from the same pot. The Farmer hands his barley to a man he's never met. His sister weaves cloth she'll never wear. The Counter writes it down. The Carrier moves it. The Maker has a bench in the goddess's workshop, casting copper for people far above him. And the Keeper lives behind a wall, with guards.

They depend on people outside their own households now. Some skills still overlap. But no single house can provide everything this way of life requires.

By 2350 BCE there are a dozen cities like Uruk strung along the two rivers. Each has its own god, its own king, its own wall. They trade with each other and they fight each other, mostly over water, and now and then one king bullies the rest for a few years. But nobody has ever held many cities together for long.

Then comes a man from the north. A much later legend says he started life as a baby in a basket.


# Part 3 — The First Empires

You know this story.

A woman has a baby she can't keep. She puts him in a basket made of reeds, seals it with tar so it floats, and sets it on the river. The river carries him away. Someone downstream finds him and raises him. He grows up to lead his people.

That's Moses. It's also a king named Sargon, and Sargon's version is set about a thousand years earlier. A legend written long after his death puts these words in his mouth: "My mother was a high priestess. My father I never knew. She set me in a basket of rushes and sealed the lid with tar. She cast me into the river, and the river did not drown me." A man drawing water fishes him out and raises him as a gardener, and then the goddess of love and war takes a liking to him, and he becomes king.

The surviving copies of Sargon's birth legend are from the first millennium BCE, long after the historical king. The setting of a story and the date someone wrote it down are different things. We can compare its floating basket with the Moses tradition without pretending we have a contemporary record of Sargon's infancy.

And I think there's a tell in his name. Sargon isn't a name your mother gives you. In his language it means "the king is legitimate." A man doesn't usually call himself the True King unless somebody has doubts.

Here's what we can piece together. We're on the same river plain as last time, in what's now Iraq, around 2350 BCE. Uruk is nine hundred years old. The Great Pyramid in Egypt has been standing for two centuries. And the plain is still a dozen separate cities, each with its farmland, its god and its king, fighting each other over water. Sargon turns up as a servant to the king of one of them, a city called Kish. He's the cupbearer, the man who hands the king his drink, which sounds like a waiter and is closer to chief of staff. Somehow, and nobody recorded how, the king is gone and Sargon is in charge.

Then he does something on a scale nobody in this country has managed. He marches south and takes the other cities, one after another. His inscriptions claim thirty-four battles. He beats the strongest king in the south, a man who had just bullied most of the other cities into line himself. He puts him in a wooden collar like a dog, and parades him to the gate of the chief god's temple. He keeps going until he reaches the Persian Gulf, and there, his inscription says, he washed his weapons in the sea.

Then he turns around and goes the other way, north and west, up the Euphrates, across Syria, to the mountains by the Mediterranean.

End to end it's about a thousand miles. On a modern map it's most of Iraq, a slice of Iran, eastern Syria, and the edge of Turkey and Lebanon. Egypt already had a kingdom stretching along the Nile. Here in Mesopotamia, rulers had controlled more than one city before, but Sargon's conquests brought a much larger territory under one center.

He ruled it from a city called Akkad, not far from where Baghdad is now. I can't show you a picture. Akkad has never been found. It's somewhere under the mud, the capital of Mesopotamia's first lasting empire, and nobody knows where.

So, first question. What's an empire? Here I mean one ruling power holding other peoples and territories under its authority. How is that different from a strong city that beats up its neighbors?

The cities of the plain had been fighting each other for five hundred years. When you won, you took some loot and some land, maybe some hostages, and you went home. The loser kept his own king, his own god, his own storehouse.

Sargon's conquests became a sustained project of ruling distant cities. His inscriptions describe appointed governors, military victories, and resources gathered toward Akkad. Earlier rulers had already imposed authority beyond their own city walls. The change here is the scale and duration of the effort, not the invention of conquest in a single man's lifetime.

And I want you to see how that looked from the bottom, because it's stranger than the map.

Go to the Farmer. He's in a village outside Ur, in the far south. His house is the same house. Mud brick, dirt floor, grain jars. His tools are the tools his grandfather used. The god in the temple down the road is the god who has always been there.

One thing has changed. It's the man who comes for the barley.

It used to be a man from Ur. He spoke the Farmer's language, Sumerian, and he worked for the king of Ur, who served the god of Ur, and that was simply how the world was arranged. Now there's a governor who was sent from somewhere five weeks upriver, by a king the Farmer will never lay eyes on. The governor speaks a different language at home, one called Akkadian, which is no relation at all to Sumerian. It's a distant cousin of Hebrew and Arabic. The barley still goes onto the barge. But it goes further now, to feed people the Farmer has never heard of.

Picture what that change asks of a household. The grain must still be threshed, measured, and carried out. Someone has to argue about the amount, find labor for the load, and decide what remains for the family. The new ruler can be remote while the demand is close enough to put a hand into the grain jar.

A ruler from outside wasn't an unimaginable novelty. But for this household, authority now reaches much farther beyond the familiar city and its fields.

Second question. How do you run a place you've never seen?

Sargon's officials could draw on generations of city government. Now they had to adapt that experience to a much larger territory, with more languages, longer journeys, and more places that might refuse an order.

How do you support that authority? One of Sargon's inscriptions says that five thousand four hundred men ate bread in front of him every day. Scholars have read that as a body of troops, or as a broader royal household. It does not give us a secure head count for the world's first standing army. But either reading brings us back to the storehouse: a king boasting about power is also boasting about how many people he can feed.

How do you make the accounts from one province mean something in another? You give everyone the same measures. A later king of this family issued a standard basket for the whole empire, so that a measure of barley was the same in the north as in the south.

How do you talk to all these people? You pick one language for business. That was Akkadian, written with the same wedge-shaped marks the Counter's line had invented for Sumerian. The Counter now works in two languages and serves a king he's never met.

And how do you get people who worship different gods to accept you? For that, Sargon used his daughter.

Her name is Enheduanna, and she's the person I want you to follow through the first half of this part, because she lived to see this empire through four reigns.

Ur, down in the south, was one of the holiest cities in the old country. Its temple belonged to the moon god. The most important religious office in that temple was the high priestess, and whoever held it was, in the theology, the god's wife on earth. Sargon made his daughter high priestess of the moon at Ur.

You can see what he was doing. The southerners had their own gods and their own priests, and those priests had every reason to hate him. So he puts his own child at the top of their most sacred temple. The message is that the new king isn't replacing your god. Your god has accepted the new king's family. It also puts a person he trusts in a city five weeks from his capital.

We know what she looked like, roughly. In the 1920s the same Leonard Woolley who dug the royal tombs found a stone disc in the ruins of the priestess's house at Ur. It had been smashed in ancient times and he pieced it together. It shows a woman in a long tiered robe overseeing an offering, and the inscription on the back names her: Enheduanna, wife of the moon god, daughter of Sargon.

But the disc isn't why she matters. She's remembered as a writer.

Under Enheduanna's name we have fierce, personal hymns to the goddess Inanna. They survive in copies made centuries after her lifetime, and scholars disagree about how much of the poetry goes back to her. Her historical position is secure; the relationship between that woman and every line attributed to her is harder to establish. The works made her name part of a literary tradition, not just a royal family tree.

Notice whose daughter she is. The Counter's tool, the thing invented to track barley, has just been picked up by the Keeper's family and used to say how a person feels. Nobody planned that either.

Meanwhile the empire is doing what empires do, which is pull things toward the middle.

Sargon boasted that ships from distant lands reached his capital. One trading partner was Meluhha, generally identified with the Indus civilization, far to the east. There is a later seal, from around the end of the third millennium BCE, belonging to a man called Shu-ilishu. Its inscription calls him an interpreter of Meluhha. It doesn't put him at Sargon's own dock. It gives us something more modest and wonderfully human: someone whose job was to make that distant trade understandable.

Someone spoke both sides of a conversation that we can now recover from only one side. To him it was work.

That's the Carrier's world now. His line isn't hauling barges for one temple anymore. They're moving goods between civilizations.

And what they're moving, more than anything, is metal. By now more and more of the smiths are using the tin recipe in place of the arsenic one. Nine parts copper, one part tin: bronze. It's harder, it casts better, and it doesn't cripple the Maker. But there's no tin in Iraq. There's none anywhere near. It comes from mountains far to the east or north, at the far end of a chain of middlemen. The best weapons in that standing army depend on a road that begins somewhere no one in the empire has ever been.

Which raises a question I'd like you to keep at the back of your mind for a couple of hours. Iron ore is everywhere. It's in practically every range of hills from Spain to India. Nobody has to haul it a thousand miles. So why are these people building their whole world on a metal that needs a rare ingredient from the edge of the map? Why is this the Bronze Age? I'll answer it when we get to the top of that world. Just notice that it's odd.

Sargon dies after about fifty years on the throne. Two of his sons rule after him and hold it together. Then his grandson takes over, and the grandson's name is Naram-Sin.

Naram-Sin is the first ruler in this story who was born into an empire. He never knew a world without it, and he was good at the job. He pushed the borders further than his grandfather had.

Then nearly everything rose against him at once. The cities of the south and the cities of the north both revolted, with their own kings, in the same year. By his own account he fought nine battles in that one year and won every one.

And here is what happened next, as he had it inscribed on the base of a copper statue that was found by a road crew in northern Iraq in 1975. After the nine victories, it says, the people of his city asked the gods to make him the god of their city. And the gods agreed. And they built him a temple.

From then on he writes his name with the sign that marks a god. On his great victory monument, which is in Paris now, he's shown climbing a mountain over the bodies of his enemies, twice the size of his own soldiers, wearing a helmet with horns on it. Horns were what gods wore.

Third question. Can a living man be a god?

In Egypt, yes, and we'll get there in a minute. In Iraq it was new, and it was shocking. Their own tradition was strict about it. They kept a list of every king since the beginning of time, and it starts with the line "When kingship was lowered from heaven." Kingship was a thing the gods lent out, to one city at a time. The early kings on the list reign for tens of thousands of years apiece, but even they are borrowers. The king serves the god. He isn't one.

Naram-Sin had just said the rule didn't apply to him.

The poetry attributed to Enheduanna also tells a story of political violence at Ur. Its speaker says a rebel has forced her from her religious office. We cannot turn all its details into a securely dated eyewitness account of Naram-Sin's revolt, but we can hear how it presents the experience of losing power.

The voice in the poem is no longer simply a royal daughter occupying an important office. She is someone pleading for that position and her good name to be restored. The institution that made her powerful has also made her vulnerable.

One of those poems tells the story. In it she says the rebel has driven her out of the temple, that she's been made to fly like a swallow from the window. She says "my good name is destroyed." And then, in the middle of a hymn to a goddess, the speaker names herself. She says: "I am Enheduanna. Let me speak to you."

The poem presents a restoration of her position. That is the story the work tells; the political sequence behind it is less certain.

What holds my attention is the combination: a real royal daughter in a powerful religious office, and a later literary tradition that speaks in her name with extraordinary force. We don't need to know every stage of that tradition to hear a person rather than another total of barley.

That's the last we see of her. The rest of this part happens after her time.

Fourth question, and it's the one this series is really about. Why do empires fall?

Within a couple of generations of Naram-Sin, Akkad was gone. His son held on. After that it was four kings in three years, and then a mountain people called the Gutians were raiding the plain and the cities were on their own again.

About a century later, somebody wrote down why. It's a poem called the Curse of Akkad, and its explanation is simple. Naram-Sin got above himself. He wanted to rebuild the temple of the chief god and the omens said no. He waited seven years. Then he lost patience, marched on the temple, and wrecked it. The gods were furious, and they sent the mountain people down on the plain as a punishment. The poem ends with a curse: may your canals fill with silt, may grass grow on your towpaths.

As history it doesn't hold up. The empire outlasted Naram-Sin by a generation. But I want you to notice the shape of it, because you already know it. The great man reaches too far, and the gods bring him down. Fifteen hundred years later the Greeks built their tragedies on that. The Hebrew prophets used it. You use it. The next time some big institution collapses and your first thought is to look for the arrogant man at the top, you're repeating a story that priests in Iraq pressed into clay four thousand years ago, about a king who wore horns.

So what did happen?

There are physical clues to environmental stress around this period: dust in marine sediments, changes in settlement, and records preserved in caves and lakes. Some point to severe drying in parts of the region around 2200 BCE. They do not give us a single weather report for every province, and the timing of the Akkadian state's political decline does not fit every climatic record neatly.

Drought may have made existing conflicts and provisioning problems harder to manage. That is a plausible connection, not a complete explanation recovered from a ring of dust. Different districts could face different pressures, and the documents and the ground do not let us isolate one cause of the empire's end.

Remember the possibility: a difficult harvest can be harder to survive when conflict and disrupted supplies are already wearing down a state's resources.

Now a side trip to Egypt, where a different state faced its own period of fragmentation. The comparison is useful, but we should not assume that similar-looking endings prove a single simultaneous cause.

Egypt had been a single kingdom for seven hundred years by now. Its king wasn't the steward of a god. He was one, from the day he was crowned, and nobody found that shocking. And by Sargon's day the Egyptians had already built the thing they're known for. The Great Pyramid went up around 2560 BCE. When Sargon was born it had already been standing for about two hundred years.

Here's a simple question about it. Who built it? Everyone has heard it was slaves in chains. It wasn't that.

In 2013, at an ancient harbor on the Red Sea, archaeologists found a bundle of papyrus scrolls. They're the oldest written papyri ever discovered, and they turned out to be a logbook. It was kept by a man named Merer, who was the foreman of a crew of about forty, and his crew's job was to haul limestone for the Great Pyramid.

It's a wonderfully dull document. Day after day: we loaded stone at the quarry. We sailed downriver. We spent the night at such-and-such. We unloaded at the building site. We went back. He records that the crew was paid in bread and beer. It's a working man's diary from inside the construction of the Great Pyramid, and what it shows is organized crews doing a season's work.

And next to the pyramids, archaeologists found the town the builders lived in. It had bakeries turning out bread on an industrial scale. The bone dumps show that the workers ate beef, a great deal of it. Their skeletons have broken bones that were set and healed, which means somebody was giving them medical care. They were organized in gangs, and the gangs scratched their names on the blocks. One was called the Friends of Khufu, after the king. Another was the Drunkards of Menkaure.

So that's the Farmer's kind of work in Egypt. He's called up for a season, and I doubt he had much say in it. He's fed well, he hauls stone for a god-king alongside men from his own village, and they give their team a silly name.

Now put Egypt beside Akkad. Late in the third millennium BCE, the kingdom that had built the great pyramids broke into competing regional powers. Poor Nile floods may have added to its troubles. One provincial governor boasted in his tomb that he had kept his district fed while other people starved. That is a ruler telling posterity why he deserves to be remembered, not a survey of the whole country. But it tells us what he wanted credit for: keeping food available when other authorities could not.

The Egyptian and Iraqi disruptions belong to the same broad period. Some chronologies bring them close together, but the dates do not give us two synchronized disasters. I think the comparison is worth making anyway. Environmental pressure could make it harder for either government to hold its provinces together. Whether the same climatic change helped weaken both remains an open question.

Egypt eventually reunited. For now, come back to Iraq.

Akkad was gone, but the idea wasn't. Once somebody has ruled all the cities, every ambitious king knows it can be done.
