It took about a hundred years. Around 2112 BCE a king of Ur, Enheduanna's old city, pulled the south back together. He built the great stepped temple tower at Ur, which is still standing, about two hundred miles south of Baghdad. He issued the oldest set of laws we have, about three centuries before Hammurabi, the Babylonian king whose laws we will meet next, and in his laws you mostly pay fines.

His son ruled for forty-eight years and I can't resist telling you about him. He claimed, in a hymn he had written about himself, that he once ran from one holy city to another and back in a single day, through a hailstorm, to celebrate a festival in both. That's about two hundred miles. He also claimed to be the best scribe in the land. And he, too, declared himself a god. Naram-Sin's idea, the one that was supposed to have doomed Akkad, had stuck.

What this kingdom was better at than anyone before it was paperwork. More than a hundred thousand clay tablets survive from about fifty years of its government. It's one of the best-documented half centuries in all of ancient history, and nearly all of it is receipts.

Listen to what they tracked. In one province, the state weaving sheds employed about fifteen thousand women. Each was owed a fixed amount of barley a month, so much oil a year, so much wool. When a weaver died, they wrote it down and stopped the ration. When a sheep died, the shepherd had to turn in the skin to prove he hadn't sold it.

The women doing the Farmer's sister's kind of work appear in these administrative records through obligations, rations, and labor. Sometimes ancient records do preserve individual names. What we usually lack is an account in the woman's own voice of the life behind the entry.

It lasted about a century.

The trouble came from three directions.

From the west, herders. They were called Amorites, and they'd been drifting in from the Syrian steppe for generations, drawn by the green fields. One king of Ur built a wall right across the country between the two rivers to stop them, a hundred and something miles long. The wall had a name, and the name tells you everything about how they felt. They called it Keeps the Nomads Away.

It didn't keep the nomads away.

From inside, a betrayal. Under the last king of Ur, the harvests failed and the price of grain in the capital went up sixty times over. The king sent one of his senior officials north with a boatload of silver to buy grain. The official bought it. Then he wrote back that the roads were too dangerous to ship it, and he'd need to be made governor of the city he was in to keep it safe. And then of the next city. Within a few years he was a king, and Ur's grain was his.

The exchange survives in later copies, part of the literary memory of Ur's fall. It presents a king unable to make an official deliver urgently needed grain. Whether every accusation is reliable or not, the practical problem is clear: commanding a shipment and getting it to the city are different things.

The enemy showed up anyway. In 2004 BCE an army from Elam, the kingdom in the hills of southwestern Iran, came down and sacked Ur. They looted the temple of the moon, where Enheduanna had lived. They took the last king away in chains, and he died in Iran.

And afterward someone at Ur wrote a poem. It's called the Lament for Ur, and it's four hundred lines of grief. The goddess of the city walks through the ruins weeping. The gates are broken. The dead lie in the streets where the festivals used to be. Storms have blown the city away, she says, and she has nowhere to live.

They'd invented a kind of poem for the death of a city. They would need it again.

One more thing was dying in these centuries. People were giving up speaking Sumerian at home. We can't put a date on it. The language of the first cities, of the first writing, of Enheduanna's hymns, stopped being anyone's mother tongue. It lived on in the schools. For the next two thousand years every educated person in Iraq had to learn it, the way educated Europeans once had to learn Latin, and it was no one's native speech.

So take stock of the family at the year 2000.

The Keeper's line has ruled an empire twice and lost it twice, and has learned to call itself divine. That idea can't be unlearned.

The Counter's line can now write a poem, a law, a letter and a lie, in two languages, one of them dead.

The Carrier's line has been to India.

The Maker's line is casting bronze, and can't make it without tin from the end of the earth.

And the Farmer has learned that the man who takes his barley can change overnight. What changes for him is how far it travels, and whether anything comes back in a bad year.

For the next couple of centuries nobody holds the whole plain. There are rival kingdoms, and merchants, and new peoples moving in. And in that gap, for the first time, we get to read ordinary people's mail.


# Part 4 — The Merchants and the Lawgiver

A woman is writing to her husband, and she's annoyed.

He's far away, doing business in another country. The cloth she makes travels out to him with the caravans; complaints come back. The pieces are too small. The quality isn't right. She has some answers for him.

Her replies survive. In one letter she discusses the size of the pieces and how much wool she has put into them. In another, she wants to know who is in his house finding fault with her cloth. These are separate letters, but the frustration runs through them. She is managing the work at home, and the man abroad keeps sending instructions.

Her name is Lamassi. His is Pushu-ken. They lived about three thousand nine hundred years ago, and we have dozens of their letters, and those are the first private voices in this story. Up to now, everything I've read you was written by a temple or a king. This is a married couple arguing about work.

It's about 1900 BCE. Ur fell a century ago. Nobody rules the whole of Iraq now. But the roads between the cities are open, and people are using them.

So, first question. How do you mail a letter when there's no paper?

You take a lump of clean clay about the size of your palm and you write on it with the cut end of a reed while it's damp. You let it dry. Then you wrap it in a thin second skin of clay, like a pie crust, and on the outside you write who it's for and roll your personal seal across it. That's the envelope. To read the letter you have to break it, so if it arrives cracked, you know to wonder who's been in your mail. Archaeologists have found some that were never opened. They can X-ray them now and read the letter inside.

Then you hand it to a man with a donkey.

Lamassi lives at Assur, on the Tigris in northern Iraq. Pushu-ken is at Kanesh, on the plateau of central Turkey. Between the two homes lie hundreds of miles of road, river crossings, and mountains. A journey can take weeks. The letter travels with people already moving goods; a reply needs a messenger going the other way. Imagine waiting for an answer while the wool still has to be bought and the household still has to eat. Later Assyrian kings will rule a vast empire from this northern homeland. For now our story is about a merchant city and families doing business abroad.

What are these people doing so far apart?

Remember the problem. Bronze needs tin, and tin comes from far away. Around 1900 BCE the tin is coming from somewhere deep in Asia, by way of Iran, and it arrives in Assur. Meanwhile, the kingdoms of central Turkey have copper, and silver, and gold. There is evidence for local tin production in Anatolia too. But imported tin was central to this trading business.

Assur is sitting between a place with tin and a place that will pay nearly anything for it.

So the merchants of Assur buy tin, and they buy fine wool cloth, some of it woven by their own wives and daughters. They pack it on donkeys. A donkey carries about a hundred and fifty pounds: tin in sealed bags on each side, cloth on top. They walk it seven hundred miles to Kanesh. And there the tin sells for about twice what they paid for it, and the cloth for three times.

That's before the costs: the donkeys, the drivers, the tolls, the interest, and the loads that never arrive. But it's the whole business. Buy in Assur, sell high in Kanesh, carry the silver home, and do it again. A man might do it for thirty years and never go home at all, which is why his wife is writing to him.

It was big. Going by the surviving records, the caravans moved something like a hundred tons of tin and a hundred thousand bolts of cloth in a single generation. Every pound of it on the back of a donkey.

This is the Carrier's line, and look how far it's come. In the first house he was the brother who walked to get volcanic glass. In Uruk he pulled a barge for the temple. Now he's in business for himself.

And the setup at the far end is the cleverest part.

The traders from Assur didn't conquer Kanesh. They couldn't have. They rented. They had a neighborhood at the foot of the hill, below the local king's palace, and inside that neighborhood they ran their own affairs. They had their own courts, their own rules, their own assembly. They paid the local king his taxes and gave him first pick of the goods, and in return he promised to protect the caravans and to pay compensation if one was robbed on his roads. It was written into treaties.

I think of it as an embassy with a homeowners' association.

Now here's what makes these people worth stopping for. Assur, the home city, wasn't run by a king in the usual sense. It had a ruler, but his title was "steward of the god," and many of the real decisions were made by an assembly of the heads of the big merchant families. Each year was named after an official who was picked by drawing lots. It was something like a small trading republic with a king attached, four thousand years ago, and almost nobody has heard of it, because it never built a pyramid. It left paperwork.

Twenty-three thousand clay tablets have come out of the houses at Kanesh, and nearly all of them are from two generations of these families. The quarter burned around 1830 BCE, the fire baked the tablets hard, and there they sat.

Second question. What's a loan, before there are banks?

It's a loan. The contracts name the amount, the due date and the interest. Among these merchants the standard rate was thirty percent a year. They could afford it, because the trade earned more.

They had something more sophisticated too. A dozen investors would each put gold into what they called a sack. One trader ran the sack for ten or twelve years. At the end he kept a third of the profit and the investors split the rest. If an investor wanted out early, he got his money back and nothing more. It's close to what we'd call an investment fund. The difference is that everyone in it knew everyone else, and most of them were related.

They had debt notes you could hand on to someone else to collect. They had partners, and agents, and lawsuits when partners cheated.

And they cheated on their taxes.

The local kings charged a toll on everything that came through. So there was a back road through the hills that bypassed the toll stations. The letters call it the narrow track, and they discuss it the way you'd discuss a shipping option. Is it worth it this season? Are the guards watching it?

Sometimes it went wrong. There's a letter in the archive from a merchant to his partner, warning him off. It says, in effect: so-and-so's son sent contraband to Pushu-ken, and it was caught, and the palace has seized Pushu-ken and put him in jail. The guards are strict. Please don't try to smuggle anything.

So Lamassi's husband, the one who complained about her cloth, did time.

The letters don't let us line up every complaint and arrest as one continuous domestic scene. But they do let us see how much business was being managed at the other end of the route, while the man abroad was sending instructions home.

Notice, too, that the whole business ran on other kings' land, by treaty. It was a permission.

Now look at the other end, because the men in Kanesh are only half the firm.

Lamassi is in Assur running everything else. She buys the wool. She manages the women who weave it, and she weaves herself. A good piece takes months. She arranges the donkeys, pays the export tax, deals with her husband's creditors, and raises the children, and she does it for years at a stretch with a husband who is a six-week walk away.

The family letters are sharp. One wife complains about being left with an empty house while her husband makes a life abroad. In another exchange, it is two sisters addressing their brother: he loves money, they say, and hates his own life. The relationship matters. This is a wider family trying to get an absent man to attend to obligations at home, not another quarrel between Lamassi and her husband.

They had reasons to worry. The law of these merchants allowed a man one wife in Assur and a second in Turkey, provided it was only one in each place. The contracts spell it out.

And did the wives write these letters themselves? The script the merchants used was a stripped-down version, a couple of hundred signs, enough for letters and accounts. A scholar named Cécile Michel has studied the women's letters more closely than anyone, and she thinks a good number of them were written by the women's own hands. The letters give us an unusually vivid view of writing used inside trading households, far beyond royal proclamations. The Counter's skill, invented to track a god's barley, is being used by a wife to tell her husband he's an idiot.

And while we're on people who weren't supposed to be able to write, I want to show you something that was happening off to the side in these same generations. It turns out to be the biggest thing in this part.

Between Egypt and Canaan lies the Sinai Peninsula, where Egyptians mined turquoise. People from Canaan joined the expeditions, bringing a language related to later Hebrew into a landscape covered with Egyptian inscriptions. Somewhere in this wider world of contact, people began experimenting with a different way to write.

One influential explanation places an important part of that experiment among the people working around those mines. Take a picture and use it for the first sound of the word in your own language. The word for ox was something like alef, so an ox's head could stand for its opening sound. The word for house was bet. A little picture of a house could stand for B. You no longer needed a separate sign for every thing you wanted to name.

Short inscriptions around the Sinai mines use just such a principle. Related early alphabetic inscriptions also come from Egypt itself. Their dates and the identities of their writers are debated, so we should not award the invention to a named crew we cannot identify. What matters here is the experiment: a small set of signs representing sounds, adapted from a much more elaborate writing tradition.

Turn a capital A upside down. You'll see the horns.

That's all I'll say for now. Hold onto the ox.

One thing I said I wouldn't let slide. In the same archive rooms, in the same handwriting, there are bills of sale for people. A girl, bought for so much silver, with witnesses. Families in debt handing over a child. Lamassi's weaving women may have been hired, or may have been owned. The letters do not always give us enough information to recover each worker's legal position.

And there's one small thing in these letters to tuck away for later. Now and then the merchants mention a metal so rare that the city of Assur restricted who could trade it. It was worth forty times its weight in silver. Most scholars think it was iron, probably the kind that falls from the sky in meteorites. In 1900 BCE iron is jewelry.

And what became of Lamassi and Pushu-ken? The record doesn't give us a neat last scene with the couple together. Later letters concern their children and the division of family property, including their sister's claim to a share. The business outlived the correspondence we have been listening to. I would rather leave the end of the marriage open than invent the homecoming their letters make us hope for.

Go forward a hundred and fifty years, and south to the old city of Ur, because I can't do a part about merchants without the worst one.

His name was Ea-nasir, and he dealt in copper. He bought it at an island in the Persian Gulf and sold it in Ur. And in the ruins of what was probably his house, archaeologists found a tablet from a customer named Nanni.

Nanni had paid in advance for good copper. What he was offered, he says, was junk. He sent a servant to sort it out and Ea-nasir was rude to the man and sent him away, twice, through dangerous country. Nanni writes: "What do you take me for, that you treat somebody like me with such contempt?" And he says that from now on he'll pick out the copper himself, in his own yard, and he'll exercise his right to reject it.

That tablet is in the British Museum, and it's recognized as the oldest customer complaint in the world. A few years ago the internet found it, and Ea-nasir is now more famous than nearly every king in this series.

Here's why it deserves that. It wasn't the only one. Other letters from other unhappy customers were found in the same house. He kept them. And for that complaint to exist at all, a great deal has to be in place. Payment in advance. An agreed standard of quality. A messenger service. A right to refuse delivery. Nanni is furious because he believes the system owes him something. In four thousand years of records, that's about the most modern feeling I can find.

So that's what a loan and a deal look like. Now the darker half of the question. What happens when you can't pay?

Come back to the Farmer, because he's a borrower too, and he isn't borrowing to triple his money.

He may borrow grain because the old harvest is running out before the new one is ready. Old Babylonian documents commonly use annual rates of twenty percent for silver and about a third for barley, though actual terms vary. For a simple one-year illustration, three baskets borrowed at a third become four baskets owed. That is not a claim that every spring loan charged a full year's interest by June. The danger for this borrower is that his repayment depends on a harvest he cannot guarantee.

If the harvest is poor, he can't pay. Then the lender can take what the loan was secured on. It might be the ox, or the field. Or it might be a member of the family, sent to work in the lender's house until the debt is cleared. A child. His wife. Himself.

Debt can transfer land, labor, and bargaining power toward creditors. Kings have reasons to intervene beyond sympathy: a household stripped of its resources may no longer be able to supply taxes, soldiers, or other obligations. The private creditor's gain can become the ruler's problem.

So the kings did something I find astonishing. Every so often, usually when a new king took the throne, he announced that the debts were cancelled. All the small personal ones, the grain loans and the silver loans to farmers. Anyone who'd been handed over for debt went home. The fields went back. The clay tablets the debts were written on were broken. Business loans between merchants weren't touched, because those were investments.

We have the text of some of these decrees. They happened again and again, for centuries. The kings called it "establishing justice."

It was a reset button. A thousand years later you find the same idea in the Bible, as the Jubilee. I think it's one of the most interesting inventions of the whole Bronze Age, and hardly anyone has heard of it, because the king we remember from this period is remembered for something else. His name was Hammurabi, and he was king of Babylon.

Leave Nanni's complaint for a moment and go back a few decades, to the beginning of Hammurabi's reign. We are on the river plain again, about a century after the merchant households we began with. When Hammurabi took the throne in 1792 BCE, Babylon was a small kingdom on the Euphrates with bigger neighbors on every side. You've heard of Babylon. At that point hardly anyone had.

We know what the map looked like because of a letter. It was written by an official to his king, and it says: there is no king who is strong on his own. Ten or fifteen kings follow the king of Babylon. As many follow the king of Larsa. As many follow two others. And twenty follow the king of Aleppo.

That's the world of 1770 BCE in one paragraph. Nobody is on top. Everyone needs allies.

That letter was found in a city called Mari, two hundred and fifty miles up the Euphrates from Babylon, in what's now eastern Syria, and Mari is where I want to take you, because its archive is as good as the merchants', except that it's the kings' mail.

Some of it is very human. A few years earlier Mari had been conquered by a tough old warlord from the north, who put his younger son on its throne. The son turned out to like wine and women more than work. And we have the father's letters. In one he writes: are you a child? Is there no beard on your chin? He points out that while the boy lies around among the women, his older brother is out winning battles.

That's a king, in 1780 BCE, writing the letter every disappointed father has wanted to write.

When the old man died, Mari was taken back by the family he'd thrown out. The new king was named Zimri-Lim, and his mail is some of the liveliest we have from any ancient ruler. His palace had more than two hundred and sixty rooms and painted walls, and visitors came from other kingdoms just to see it. His letters are full of his daily business. A lion was caught on a rooftop in one of his towns, and the governor wrote to ask what to do with it. He built an ice house, to have cold drinks in summer. His wife ran the palace when he travelled and wrote to him about everything.

And his great ally was Hammurabi. For years they exchanged troops, and intelligence, and gifts. Zimri-Lim's soldiers fought in Hammurabi's wars. His ambassadors in Babylon sent home reports of what Hammurabi had said at dinner.

Then, late in his reign, Hammurabi made his move. In about five years he knocked out his rivals one by one: first the big kingdom to the south, then the one to the east. And in 1761 he turned on Mari.

We don't know what happened to Zimri-Lim. He just stops. What we know is that the Babylonian army occupied the palace, and that Babylonian clerks then spent months going through the archive. They sorted the tablets into baskets and labelled them. We have the labels. They took away the letters they wanted, which seem to have been the ones from other great kings. Then, two years later, the soldiers came back, stripped the palace, and burned it.

The fire baked what was left. In 1933 some men digging a grave on a hill by the Euphrates hit a stone statue, and the French archaeologists who followed found twenty-five thousand tablets in the ruins. Everything I've just told you about the lion and the ice house and the lazy son comes out of that fire.

That's the man who is remembered as the great lawgiver.

Third question. Where does law come from?

You've probably heard that it comes from him. Near the end of his life he had a pillar of black stone set up, seven feet tall. At the top it shows him standing before the god of the sun, who is the god of justice. Below are two hundred and eighty-two rulings, carved in fine script. It's in the Louvre in Paris.

"An eye for an eye" is in there. But read it closely. If a gentleman puts out the eye of another gentleman, he loses his own eye. If he puts out the eye of a commoner, he pays a fine. If it's a slave's eye, he pays the owner half the slave's price. Equal justice between equals, and a price list for everyone else.

A lot of it is about ordinary trouble. A builder puts up a house, it falls down and kills the owner, and the builder is put to death. A surgeon who operates on a gentleman and kills him loses his hand. A man who can't pay his debts may hand over his wife or his child to work it off, and here's a line I want you to hear: they serve three years, and in the fourth they go free. That's the same sickness the debt cancellations were treating.

So was this the law? Scholars argue about it. We have thousands of court records from his reign and the years after, and not one judge ever cites that stone. It wasn't the first collection of its kind either. We met one three hundred years older. Whatever use the courts made of it, I think the pillar is first of all an advertisement. It's a king at the end of his life saying: look at the kind of order I kept.

Hammurabi is famous for the wrong thing. The stone made him the great lawgiver. The cancelled debts did more for more people, and so did the dull habit of writing down what was decided. And the man himself spent his best years as a schemer who waited thirty years and then ate his neighbors.

One more thing about that pillar. It didn't stay in Babylon. Six hundred years later a king from Iran carried it off as a trophy, and that's where it was dug up. Keep that in mind. We'll meet the thief.

The last stretch of this part is a bridge to the next one, and it starts with a fourth question. Why did the wheel take so long?

It seems like the most obvious invention there is. But the wheel was never the hard part. The axle was. A wheel has to turn freely on a fixed rod without wobbling and without sticking, and that's fine carpentry. And a cart is no use without something heavy to haul, an animal trained to pull it, and ground flat enough to roll on. All of that came together around 3500 BCE, and the first wheels were solid discs made of planks, on heavy carts pulled by oxen at walking pace.

For a wheel to be fast it has to be light, and that means spokes: a rim, a hub, and thin rods between. That's fine woodworking, and it appears about 2000 BCE. It doesn't appear in any of the cities. It shows up on the grasslands east of the Ural Mountains, among herders who had no writing and no kings. They buried their dead with two-wheeled carts, and the wheels left their prints in the soil of the graves, spokes and all. Those same people had been breeding a new, stronger kind of horse.

A light cart, two spoked wheels, two fast horses. Put a driver in it and an archer beside him. That's a chariot, and nothing on foot can catch it or get away from it.

Over the next three centuries it spread south into every kingdom we've met. And think about what it takes to keep one. A horse trainer. A stable. A wheelwright, a joiner, a harness maker. An archer who's practiced since he was a boy. A chariot is like a fighter jet. No farmer owns one. It takes a rich household to keep one, and a king to keep a few hundred.

So the Maker gets a new trade: he builds chariots. And the Keeper gets a weapon that hardly anyone else can afford. From here on a king's strength is counted in chariots, and his chariots are counted in what his palace can pay for.

The political map was changing too. In 1595 BCE, an army from the north reached Babylon.

Up in central Turkey, in the same country where the merchants of Assur once had their quarter, a new kingdom had formed. We call its people the Hittites. In 1595 their king led his army out of the highlands, down the length of the Euphrates, about eight hundred miles, and sacked Babylon. Hammurabi's city, five generations after Hammurabi. Then he turned round and went home with the loot, and his brother-in-law murdered him.

He didn't try to hold Babylon. He couldn't have. But everyone took note. An army could now arrive from a place that wasn't on your map.

Babylon was picked up by a mountain people called the Kassites, who ruled it for the next four hundred years and became more Babylonian than the Babylonians. Egypt learned the same lesson another way. Families from Canaan had been settling in the Nile Delta for generations, and around 1650 their leaders took over the north of the country and ruled it for a century, with chariots. The Egyptians of the south threw them out around 1550, and kept the chariots. The Egypt that comes out of that war is the one with the famous names, and it has an army and wants to use it.

And there's one more part of the map I've been neglecting, and it's the part you probably know best.

Go west across the sea, to the islands between Turkey and Greece. On the biggest of them, Crete, there's by this time a civilization with palaces. The biggest is at a place called Knossos. It had hundreds of rooms on several floors around a central court, with storerooms and workshops and stairways. It was an administrative center, like the temple at Uruk. They kept accounts on clay in a script nobody has ever deciphered. They painted their walls with dolphins and with young men and women vaulting over the backs of bulls. Later Greeks would remember Crete as the home of a king with a maze under his house and a monster in it that was half bull.

Seventy miles north of Crete was an island with a town on it, and around 1600 BCE the island blew up. It was one of the largest volcanic eruptions of the last ten thousand years. The middle of the island collapsed into the sea. The town was buried under ash, the way Pompeii would be seventeen centuries later.

Archaeologists have been digging that town since the 1960s. The houses stand three stories high. There are wall paintings as fresh as the day they were covered: ships, swallows, boys boxing, a fisherman holding up his catch. There are indoor toilets connected to drains under the street.

No bodies have been found, and almost nothing valuable. It looks as though earthquakes came first, and the people understood, and packed up what they could carry and left before the end. Where they went, we don't know.

Crete's palaces went on for another century and more. And on the mainland of Greece another people was on the rise. At a hilltop called Mycenae they were burying their chiefs in deep shafts with gold masks over their faces and bronze swords at their sides, and around their necks, beads of amber that had come all the way from the Baltic Sea. A few generations on, people from the mainland would be running the palace at Knossos, and they'd take the Cretans' script and bend it to write their own language.

Their own language was Greek. These are the people who, in a much later poem, sail to Troy.

So where's the family, around 1500 BCE?

The Carrier is a businessman. He has investors, contracts, a tax strategy, and a wife who runs the home office.

The Counter isn't only a temple clerk now. He might be a merchant, or a merchant's wife, or someone experimenting with a few signs scratched on a rock.

The Keeper has learned to cancel debts, to carve his justice in stone, and to burn his friend's house down. He has chariots.

The Maker builds them.

And the Farmer is in debt. Sometimes a king wipes it out. Then it builds up again.

They live in different countries now and they'll never meet.

In about two hundred years, people like these will have built the most connected world there had ever been. I want to show it to you from the deck of a ship.


# Part 5 — The Brotherhood of Kings

Off the southern coast of Turkey, around the year 1300 BCE, a ship is going down.

She isn't big. About fifty feet, the length of a city bus and a bit. She's built of cedar from the mountains of Lebanon, and she's riding very low, because she's carrying ten tons of copper.

It's in three hundred and fifty-four slabs, more than fifty pounds each, cast flat with a handle at every corner so two men can carry one between them. They're stacked in overlapping rows like roof tiles. Under them is a ton of tin. Around them are a hundred and fifty big clay jars, most of them full of a sticky tree resin used for incense. There are logs of black wood from Africa. There are elephant tusks and hippopotamus teeth. There are a hundred and seventy-five round cakes of raw glass, most of them deep blue. There are ostrich eggs, and beads of amber from the Baltic Sea. There's a gold scarab with the name of the queen of Egypt on it.

Picture the practical problem of working around that cargo. Each slab is roughly the weight of a heavy suitcase. Jars have to be secured against movement; loads need to be placed so the vessel can sail safely. This is a reconstruction of the work, but the weight is real. Those beautiful objects in museum cases were once freight that somebody had to lift.

And somewhere near the bow there's a small bronze statue of a goddess with gold over her face and hands. She's there to get the ship home.

We don't know exactly how the ship was lost. Her cargo came to rest down a steep underwater slope, where it remained for more than three thousand years. The wreck gives us objects and their positions; it cannot replay the last minutes of the voyage.

In the summer of 1982 a young Turkish sponge diver named Mehmet Çakır came up and told his captain he'd seen metal biscuits with ears on the bottom. The captain knew what that meant. Archaeologists spent eleven summers and more than twenty thousand dives bringing her up.

I'm starting here because that ship is the best single picture of this age. Go through the hold. The copper is from Cyprus. The glass is Egyptian. The black wood is from south of Egypt. The amber came from the far side of Europe. The jars are from the coast of Lebanon and Israel. Nothing on her was made anywhere near where she sank, and no one country on Earth could have filled her.

You've seen this ship. She docks at Rotterdam now, and she's a quarter of a mile long.

And the family's all aboard. It's the Carrier's ship. The metal is the Maker's raw material. There was a folding wooden notebook on board with an ivory hinge, the kind you fill with wax and write on with a point, so the Counter was there, though the wax and whatever was written in it are long gone. The crew's lunch was in the wreck, figs and olives and pomegranates, and the Farmer grew that. And a cargo this size wasn't one merchant's gamble. Eleven tons of bronze in the making is enough to equip a small army. Most people who've studied her think this was a shipment from one king to another.

The wreck brings our five kinds of work together. It does not identify five particular passengers. It shows how a cargo can depend on farmers, craftspeople, record-keepers, merchants, and powerful customers who may never meet.

First question. How do you sail something like that with no compass and no engine?

You stay in sight of land whenever you can. You steer by mountains in the day and by stars at night. You sail in summer, when the weather is steady, and you stay in port in winter. And you go one way round. The winds and currents at this end of the Mediterranean favor a circuit: up the coast from Egypt past Lebanon, west along Turkey, across to Greece and Crete, down to Africa, and back along the shore to the Nile. This ship was on the Turkey leg, heading west, when she was lost.

We even have a fair idea who was on her, from what they left. There were several sets of the little stone weights a merchant uses with a balance, and they're on the standard used in Syria and Canaan. So, three or four merchants from that coast. There were two swords and some personal gear of the kind used in Greece. So, perhaps two Greeks, and since they carried swords and not weights, they may have been escorts sent to see the cargo home.

And my favorite passenger: a mouse. The excavators found the jawbone of a house mouse in the sediment, and a specialist compared it with mouse populations around the Mediterranean. It matched the mice of the Syrian coast. So that's probably where the ship last took on cargo, and we know it because of a stowaway.

Now the tin. Researchers have compared the metal in these ingots with ores from different regions, using chemical composition and isotopes. A study published in 2022 proposed sources in Central Asia and the Taurus Mountains of Turkey; other researchers have challenged those assignments. The broad point is safer than a map with a precise route drawn on it. This was an international trade in material whose origins are difficult to reconstruct, even with the cargo in our hands.

We don't have the shipment's full paperwork. Its merchants may have bought through intermediaries rather than dealing with the miners themselves. The ingots preserve the metal, not every conversation that moved it toward the coast.

To understand who that cargo was for, I have to take you back about fifty years, and then we'll go forward in order.

In 1350 BCE the world from Greece to Iran is run by a handful of great kings, and they know each other. Picture them round a table. I'll give each one a handle, and I'll use the same handle every time.

Egypt is the gold country. It has mines in the desert to the south that produce more gold than everywhere else combined, and it spends that gold on friends.

Across from Egypt, in central Turkey, is Hatti, the kingdom of the Hittites, the ones who raided Babylon. They called their own country the land of a thousand gods, because every time they conquered a people they adopted that people's gods too. They're Egypt's great rival.

Between them, in northern Syria, is Mitanni, the horse kingdom. Its kings trained the best chariot horses in the world, and here's a strange thing about them. A horse-training manual written by one of their experts counts the laps of the track in words that are close cousins of Sanskrit. A treaty of theirs is sworn by gods who also appear in the oldest hymns of India. Somehow a ruling family with roots far to the east ended up running a kingdom in Syria.

In the old country there's Babylon, under its mountain kings, selling horses and blue stone and living on its reputation as the oldest school in the world.

In northern Iraq is Assyria, a kingdom with its old center at Assur, the city of the donkey merchants. During these generations its rulers are emerging from Mitanni's dominance and asserting themselves among the great powers. Remember the distinction: Assur is the city; Assyria is the kingdom whose power is growing around it.

Out in the water is Alashiya, the copper island. That's Cyprus.

At the far western end are the Greeks of Mycenae, who export perfumed oil and are just starting to be taken seriously.

And where all the routes cross is a port on the Syrian coast called Ugarit. It isn't a great power. It's where the great powers' goods change hands. We'll spend an evening there.

We know how these kings dealt with each other because of something that happened in 1887. A village woman in Egypt was digging in an old ruin for crumbled mud brick, which makes good fertilizer, and she turned up a pile of clay tablets. She sold them for next to nothing. They turned out to be the foreign mail of the king of Egypt: about three hundred and fifty letters to and from the other rulers of the world.

Second question. How do kings with no common language talk to each other?

Much of the correspondence was written in Babylonian, a form of Akkadian spoken in Mesopotamia. For courts such as Egypt's and the Hittites', it served as an international language learned by scribes. Think of aviation English: the shared language makes the exchange possible even when the people on either side speak different languages at home.

And they had rules. The great kings call each other "brother." It doesn't mean they like each other. It means "I recognize you as my equal." Small kings write to the great ones as "my lord, my sun," and say they throw themselves at his feet seven times and seven times more. You always know from the first line who outranks whom.

So what do the masters of the world write to each other about? Mostly three things.

The first is gold. Everyone wants Egypt's, and the phrase they all use is that in Egypt gold is as plentiful as dust. The king of the horse kingdom writes that the king of Egypt promised him statues of solid gold, and what arrived was wood with gold leaf over it. And the gold is like dust in your country, he says. So why did that cause you such pain?

The second is marriage, and here's the third question. How do you marry someone you've never seen, who lives three months away and doesn't speak your language?

There was a whole procedure. Envoys went to look the girl over. There was a ceremony where oil was poured on her head. There was a list of her dowry down to the last comb. Then she travelled, with an escort of hundreds, and she never went home again.

But it only went one way. Everyone sent daughters to Egypt. Egypt never sent one back. When the king of Babylon asked for an Egyptian princess, the answer came: "From time immemorial, no daughter of the king of Egypt is given to anyone." And the king of Babylon's reply is one of my favorite lines from the ancient world. Then send me any beautiful woman, he says, as if she were your daughter. Who's going to say she isn't a princess?

The same king complains that his sister was sent to Egypt years ago and his envoys can't get anyone to confirm she's still alive.

The third thing is complaints. You sent no gift. You sent a smaller gift than you sent my father. Your envoy was rude to my envoy. You kept my man waiting.

One of those complaints I can't leave out. The king of Babylon had been ill, and the king of Egypt hadn't sent to ask how he was. He was offended, and he says so. Then, he writes, his own envoy explained to him that Egypt is a very long way off, too far for the news to have got there and a get-well message to have come back. And the king says he asked the Egyptian envoy whether that was true, and it was, and so he isn't angry any more.

Think about that. One of the most powerful men alive had to ask a messenger how big the world was.

And there's a letter in that archive from the rising Assyrian kingdom in northern Iraq. Its king writes to Egypt for the first time, on his own account, to introduce himself and send a chariot and two white horses. The king of Babylon found out and was livid. Those people are my subjects, he wrote to Egypt. If you love me, send them home with nothing.

Egypt didn't. A new chair had been pulled up to the table.

Now, the reason those letters survived is that they were filed in a city that was built in a hurry and abandoned in a hurry, and the man who built it is one of the strangest rulers in history.

He came to the throne of Egypt in 1353 BCE under the name Amenhotep, which means "the god Amun is content." Amun was the great god of Egypt. His temple was the richest institution in the country. It owned land and ships and tens of thousands of workers.

Within five years the new king had turned on him. He announced that there was one god worth worshipping, the disc of the sun, which he called the Aten. He changed his own name to Akhenaten, "useful to the Aten." He closed the old temples and sent men with chisels up and down Egypt to cut Amun's name out of the walls. Later they started cutting out the word "gods" where it appeared in the plural.

And he left the capital. He picked a stretch of empty desert by the Nile where nothing had ever stood, and he had a city built there for thirty thousand people in about four years. They did it by cutting the stone into small blocks that one man could carry on his shoulder.

People have wanted to make him a hero for a long time: the first man to believe in one god, a thousand years ahead of his age. Sigmund Freud wrote a book suggesting that Moses was one of his followers. More recently historians have gone the other way and called it a power grab, a king breaking the priests who were rich enough to rival him.

I don't fully buy either one. I think he believed it. The hymn to the sun that was written at his court reads like the work of someone who meant it. I also think it's no accident that his one god spoke only through him, and that the temples he closed were the only institution in Egypt that could tell a king no. Both can be true of the same man.

Now look away from the royal portraits and out to the city's cemeteries. Excavators have recovered hundreds of ordinary people. The burial grounds do not all tell the same story. At the North Tombs Cemetery, the sample is strikingly young: almost everyone whose age could be closely estimated died between five and twenty-five. Skeletal studies also reveal physical strain and poor health. They cannot tell us the exact load each person carried, but the contrast with the royal image of abundance is hard to miss.

That's another view of the city of the sun, from the people who had to live and work beneath it.

Meanwhile his empire in Syria was coming loose, and we can listen to it happen. His subject king at the port of Byblos, on the coast of Lebanon, wrote to him about sixty times. It's always the same letter. My neighbors are taking my villages. My farmers have run away. Send archers. Why don't you answer? I am like a bird in a trap, he says, here in Byblos.

At one point Egypt wrote back, and the reply amounts to: why do you write to me more than all my other governors put together?

No archers came. In the end his own brother locked him out of the city, and the letters stop.

Akhenaten died after seventeen years. Within a generation his city was empty, his temples had been pulled down, and his name had been cut out of the records so thoroughly that for three thousand years nobody knew he'd existed. The filing cabinet with the foreign letters was left behind in the empty office, and that's the only reason we have them.

He left a son, about nine years old. The boy had been named Tutankhaten, "living image of the Aten." His advisers changed it. They put the old god back, in the name and in the temples. He became Tutankhamun.

That's who he is. The gold mask everybody has seen belongs to the child of the heretic, whose whole short reign was spent undoing his father's.

He died at about nineteen, with no surviving children. And then the palace did something no one would have believed.

Up in Turkey, the king of the Hittites was on campaign in Syria when a messenger arrived from Egypt with a letter from a queen whose husband had just died. The Hittite records don't give her name. Most historians think she was Tutankhamun's widow, and I'll go with that. Her letter is quoted in those records. "My husband is dead. I have no son. They say you have many sons. Give me one of yours, and he will be my husband, and he will be king of Egypt."

The Hittite king didn't believe it. The records say he told his council that nothing like this had ever happened to him in his life. Egypt didn't even send out its daughters. Now it was offering him the throne. He sent a man to Egypt to find out whether it was a trick.

Her reply came back in the spring, and you can still hear how insulted she was. "Why do you say, they are deceiving me? If I had a son, would I have written to a foreign country in a way that humiliates me and my country?"

So he sent a son. And the prince died on the way. The Hittites said he was murdered, and they were probably right. There were men in Egypt who had no intention of taking orders from a foreigner, and one of them was on the throne within weeks.

Let me stop for a what-if, because it's one of the great ones. Suppose the prince had arrived. A Hittite on the throne of Egypt, with his father ruling Turkey and Syria. The two strongest states in the world would have been joined in one family. Would it have held? I doubt it. Egypt's priests and generals would have had a foreign boy in their hands, a long way from home. But it's the nearest those two powers ever came to becoming one, and it turned on whether a young man survived a journey. Nobody can know how it would have gone. What we know is that he didn't arrive.

The Hittite king went to war over it. He attacked Egyptian territory in Syria and marched his prisoners home.

By the Hittites' own account, the prisoners were sick. Whatever they had spread through Turkey and it didn't stop. It killed the king. It killed his heir a year later. It was still killing people twenty years on, when a younger son was on the throne, and that son wrote a series of prayers that are among the most affecting things to come down to us from this age.

He doesn't boast. He tells the gods his country is dying. The men who plowed the gods' fields are dead, he says, and the women who ground the flour for the gods' bread are dead. He's had the archives searched to find out what his family did to deserve this. And he's found it: his father broke a sworn treaty when he attacked Egypt. So he says it. "It is so. We have done it."

Follow the chain. A royal marriage, the one tool these kings trusted above all others, failed once. The failure killed a prince, started a war, and loosed a plague that ran for twenty years. The roads that carried the tin and the brides carried the disease too. Nobody had put that on the bill.

There's something else in that boy's tomb I've been waiting to show you, because it answers a question I asked you two hours ago.

Among the gold was a dagger with an iron blade. The iron came from a meteorite. It was one of the most precious things he owned.

So here's the question from the days of Sargon. Iron ore is in practically every range of hills. Usable tin deposits are much less evenly spread, often far from the places making bronze. Why did these people build their world on bronze?

There are two reasons. The first surprised me. Bronze was better. When you smelt iron ore in a simple furnace you don't get anything like steel. You get a spongy lump of soft metal that has to be hammered for hours, and a blade made from it is softer than a good bronze one and takes a worse edge. Making it hard means working carbon into it and quenching it, and nobody had that worked out reliably. There's a letter from a Hittite king of this period, answering another ruler who'd asked him for iron. He says there's no good iron in his storehouse at the moment, that it's a bad season for making it, and that for now he's sending one dagger blade. One.

The second reason is simpler. Bronze worked. The tin was arriving. The copper was arriving. Every smith from Greece to Babylon knew the recipe, and every king could get the ingredients as long as the ships and the caravans kept moving.

That was the trade these people made. They took the better metal, and the price was that they depended on a supply chain no one of them controlled. For three hundred years it looked like a very good trade.

Several decades later, Egypt and the Hittites fought at Kadesh, a fortified city beside the Orontes River in what is now Syria. Most of the detailed battle story comes from Ramses's own inscriptions and pictures. They were made to celebrate him. We can follow that account without mistaking it for a neutral report from both armies.

The king of Egypt is Ramses the Second. He's about twenty-five and he's been on the throne five years. He marches north into Syria with four divisions, about twenty thousand men, to take a fortress city called Kadesh. The divisions are a day apart on the road, and Ramses is out in front with the first.

Near the city his men pick up two local herders, who say they've come to change sides. They tell him the Hittite king is terrified of him and is hanging back a hundred and twenty miles to the north. Ramses is delighted. He hurries ahead with one division and pitches camp beside Kadesh.

Then his patrols bring in two more prisoners. These are Hittite scouts. They're beaten until they talk, and what they say is that the two herders were plants. The Hittite king isn't a hundred and twenty miles away. He's on the other side of the city, behind the hill it's built on, with his whole army, including more chariots than anyone has ever put in the field.

Ramses sends riders to hurry up the divisions behind him. It's too late. The Hittite chariots come across the river and hit the second division while it's strung out on the march, and scatter it. Then they turn and go straight through the Egyptian camp.

What saved him was partly luck. The Hittite chariot crews got into the camp and stopped to loot it. And a separate Egyptian force that had come up by the coast road arrived at exactly that moment. Ramses rallied what he had and held on until dark.

By the next day both armies were exhausted and neither could break the other. Ramses went home. The Hittites kept Kadesh, and the country south of it as well.

So who won? If you go by the map, the Hittites did. If you go by the walls of Egypt, Ramses did, gloriously and by himself. He had the battle carved on at least five temples. In his version his troops ran away, he prayed to Amun, and then he charged the enemy alone and drove them into the river. He's shown thirty feet tall. The Hittites are the size of mice.

He ruled for another sixty-one years and he never stopped telling that story. He's the greatest public relations man in history. He nearly got his army wiped out by believing two herders, and three thousand years later tourists stand in front of his version and take it for a victory.

About fifteen years after the battle the two kingdoms made peace, and it wasn't because they'd grown fond of each other. The Hittite king by then was the brother of the one who'd fought at Kadesh. He had taken the throne from his nephew, and the nephew had fled to Egypt. A man who's stolen a crown needs other kings to recognize him. And on the Hittites' eastern border, the Assyrian kingdom had become a formidable military rival.

So they signed a treaty. Egyptian and Hittite versions survive, preserving the same central agreement, though not identical wording. Neither will attack the other. Each will come to the other's aid. And each will send back the other's fugitives, with a clause that says the people sent back aren't to be punished or have their houses torn down. It's the oldest peace treaty between great powers that survives. There's a copy on the wall at the United Nations in New York.

The Hittite copy was sealed by two people, the king and the queen. Her name was Puduhepa and she's worth knowing. She ran the kingdom's correspondence alongside her husband and after him. When the peace was to be sealed with a marriage and Ramses complained that the bride and her dowry were slow in coming, she wrote back herself. I'll paraphrase. She asks him whether the king of Egypt owns nothing at all. She says that for him to squeeze her for more is beneath him.

Ramses gave as good as he got. When the Hittite court asked him to send an Egyptian doctor to help the king's sister have a child, he replied, in effect: I know your sister. She's fifty. No, she's sixty. Nobody can make a medicine for that. But he'd send a doctor anyway.

One of Ramses' sons spent those peaceful years looking much further back. His name was Khaemwaset, and he was high priest at Memphis, Egypt's old capital near the pyramids. On one old pyramid, an inscription credits him with preserving the name of the king who built it. By then that king had been dead for more than a thousand years. So here is an Egyptian prince looking at monuments already ancient to him, and making sure an earlier ruler's name stays attached to the stone. He made sure his own name was there too.

That's the peak. The two great powers are at peace, their rulers are teasing each other by mail, and a Hittite princess is on her way south with her escort.

Let me show you two places at that peak, because I'm going to need you to remember them.

The first is in Greece, at a palace called Pylos, on a hill above a bay in the southwest. I should be straight about the evidence. Everything we know about this office comes from its very last year, for a reason you'll hear later. But the routine was generations old. So picture a clerk at that desk around 1250, two generations before the end. He's the Counter. There are perhaps fifty people in this kingdom who can do what he does.

His desk is by the front entrance. He writes on palm-sized pieces of damp clay in the script the Greeks borrowed from Crete, and what he writes is the palace's day. Figs and grain for thirty-seven women and their children in the weaving unit. Bronze issued to the smiths in the villages, by weight, with a note of which smiths got none this season. Sheep by the tens of thousands. Chariot wheels, serviceable and unserviceable. Rowers owed by each town on the coast.

Some groups of women are identified by place names across the Aegean, in what is now Turkey. Scholars have argued that some were captives or otherwise dependent workers. The labels do not give us one clear legal status for every woman. They show people being administered through work and rations, with very little of their own story attached.

The tablets are working records, usually written on clay and left unbaked. Many concern a short period of administration rather than a permanent history. Imagine a clerk setting down a tablet after checking a delivery. It can dry hard enough to handle without becoming fired pottery. That difference will matter when we return to this archive.

The surviving Linear B records are overwhelmingly administrative. We have no surviving body of letters or poems in this script. That doesn't let us inspect every person's abilities in the kingdom, but it does show how closely the evidence for this kind of writing is tied to palace work. Lose that work and the training of new scribes becomes much harder to sustain.

Remember the shelf.

The second is at Ugarit, the port in Syria, at the end of a working day. Picture one of the men on the quay.

He's one of the Carrier's men, and he's spent the day hauling those fifty-pound copper slabs up a gangplank, so his shoulder is raw in the place where his ancestor's was raw from the tow rope. The quay behind him is piled with things that don't belong together. Copper from the island. Oil jars from Greece. Bolts of Egyptian linen. A crate of blue stone that started out in Afghanistan.

Imagine several languages being spoken around him. Ugarit's scribes used more than one language and more than one writing system. Among them was an alphabet of about thirty signs, written in wedges on clay. It was used for serious scribal work, including letters, religious texts, and accounts. Keep that in mind: alphabetic writing was already useful before the palaces of this world fell.

Put a singer in a doorway as the working day ends. We cannot recover this particular woman or her song; she belongs to our imagined evening. But a hymn to the goddess Nikkal really does survive among Ugarit's tablets, with signs interpreted as musical instructions. The archives contain more than prices and royal demands.

He thinks this is how the world is. The ships come. They've always come. His grandfather worked this quay.

So here's the family at the top.

The Keeper is a Great King who calls other Great Kings his brother, and marries their daughters, and has never met one of them.

The Counter is a clerk in a palace, writing in a language that isn't his own or keeping accounts nobody else can read.

The Carrier sails the circuit with ten tons of somebody else's copper.

The Maker can't work unless a ship comes in from Cyprus and a caravan comes in from the end of the earth, both in the same season.

And the Farmer feeds all four, and his sister is on a list.

This world offers possibilities the first household never had: specialized crafts, distant markets, ambitious literature, goods from beyond the horizon. The gains are not shared equally. A powerful ruler, an independent merchant, and a dependent weaver occupy very different positions. What connects them is the work that has to keep being done: harvests, shipments, agreements, and payments.

The people inside it knew about bad harvests, hostile neighbors, and failed deliveries. Their letters say so. What they could not know was which troubles would be overcome, as many had been before, and which institutions would not survive the next generations.

The rain is about to change.


# Part 6 — The Slow Part

Late in the thirteenth century BCE, decades after Egypt and the Hittites had made peace, an urgent letter went from the Hittite court to Ugarit, the trading kingdom on the Syrian coast.

It's an order for a ship and a crew to move a large quantity of grain from a Syrian region to a Hittite harbor. The ancient measures are not a reason to pretend we know the cargo's weight to the ton. What matters is the urgency. In effect, the letter says that the shipment is a matter of life or death.

Think about who's writing. This is Hatti, the land of a thousand gods. Fifty years earlier its chariots nearly destroyed the king of Egypt at Kadesh. It's one of the two strongest states on Earth, and it's telling a harbor town that if a boat doesn't come, people are going to die.

And the Egyptians knew. Around the same time the king of Egypt, who was the son of Ramses the Second, had it carved on a temple wall that he'd sent grain in ships "to keep alive the land of Hatti." Egypt is keeping its old enemy from starving, and bragging about it.

It hadn't come out of nowhere. A generation earlier the Hittite queen, the one who told Ramses off by mail, wrote to him during the marriage talks to explain a delay. One of her reasons, mentioned almost in passing, was that she had no grain in her lands.

So here's the first question. How does the greatest land power of the age end up begging for a boat?

To answer it I have to explain two things: what was going wrong, and what these kingdoms already knew how to survive. I'll take the second one first, which means going back to an earlier crisis.

Remember the table of great kings, and the horse kingdom in northern Syria. Mitanni. Its king wrote those letters to Egypt complaining about gold-plated statues. For a hundred years it was one of the four or five powers that ran the world.

Then it was taken apart. The Hittite king, the same one who got the letter from the Egyptian widow, beat it in war around 1340. The king of the horse kingdom was murdered by one of his own sons. The Hittites took the western half and made it a puppet. And the eastern half was swallowed over the next two generations by its own former subject, Assyria, the northern Iraqi kingdom centered on Assur.

By the time of the peace treaty the horse kingdom didn't exist. One of the pillars of the world had been removed. We aren't even sure where its capital was.

The rest of the international order did not collapse with it. There had been war, displacement, and a struggle over who would control the former kingdom. But routes could be redirected and new rulers could take over relationships. Assyria gained a place among the great powers. Mitanni's disappearance showed that a major political break did not have to end every connection around it.

That's the lesson I think about most in this whole story, because it was true and it was the wrong one. Other kingdoms and routes remained strong enough to carry on after the horse kingdom fell. The routes could shift because there were strong kingdoms to shift through. What nobody had tested was what happens when the parts fail together.

A court looking back from the peace treaty of 1259 BCE could point to a great power's fall and see that trade and diplomacy had continued. That was a reason for confidence, though not a promise that the next crisis would end the same way.

Now follow the environmental evidence forward, all the way to the years around 1200 BCE. After that we will return to the decisions kings were making in the preceding decades. The evidence doesn't arrive in the order an ancient household would have experienced it.

It starts with the weather, and we know about the weather because trees keep a diary.

A tree lays down one ring a year. In a good year the ring is wide. In a dry year it's narrow. Centuries after this story ends, a people in central Turkey built a huge burial mound for one of their kings and lined the chamber with whole juniper logs, and those logs were already ancient when they were cut. The rings in them run right through the years we're talking about. A team published the measurements in 2023.

They show the Hittite heartland getting drier from about 1250 BCE on. Bad years came more often. And then there's a run of three rings so thin they're hard to see. Three years in a row of drought as bad as anything in the whole record. The team's best dates are 1198, 1197 and 1196 BCE, with a margin of a few years. The people who published that are careful to say it doesn't explain everything by itself. But it's the nearest thing we have to a weather report from the end of the Bronze Age.

That isn't the only evidence. Mud from the bottom of the Sea of Galilee and from a salt lake in Cyprus holds pollen, and the pollen shows the same thing from the other side: the trees and crops thinning out and the dry-country scrub moving in, across about a century and a half.

Now go to the Farmer, on the Turkish plateau. He cannot rely on a great river to compensate for poor local rain. Even the Nile's floods could fail, but his own fields depend much more directly on rainfall here. He farms on rain. And every farming family since the first house has known one rule. You never eat the seed.

There's a jar in the corner with next year's planting in it. In a bad year you eat less. You eat the animals. You eat things you'd be ashamed to serve. The jar stays shut. Then there's a second bad year, and the animals are already gone. The tax collector comes anyway, because his tablet doesn't have a column for rainfall. And in the third year the family is sitting in front of the jar.

Eat it, and you live until spring and have nothing to plant. Don't, and you may not see spring. I'm imagining that scene, but only just. That's what three thin tree rings mean when you turn them into people. The evidence does not give us a count of households facing that exact choice. The imagined jar makes the stakes understandable; it is not another measurement in the study.

Second question, then. How do you feed an empire when the rain stops?

For a while, out of the bins. The Keeper has been storing grain for six thousand years and by now he's good at it. The Hittite capital sat on a rocky height in the middle of the Turkish plateau, more than three thousand feet up and a long way from any sea. Its defenses stretched for miles, with substantial stone foundations and mud-brick construction above, with gates guarded by carved lions, and inside there were more than thirty temples. The winters are hard there, with snow on the ground for months. It's a fine place to defend and a poor place to feed.

Excavations at Hattusa have revealed very large grain-storage installations, including some built centuries before these final crises. They show how seriously the state had invested in reserves. They do not tell us exactly how full the capital's stores were in the year of our letter. A bin's capacity and the food actually left inside it are different facts.

Reserves can carry people through a failed harvest. But a store only helps if good years come along to fill it again. If they don't, you're spending savings, and from the outside a household spending its savings looks exactly like a household doing fine. The house is the same, the meals are the same. Then one month the account is empty.

The letters and royal inscriptions show efforts to obtain grain from outside. Keep the shipments separate: the urgent Ugarit order concerns a cargo from a Syrian region, while Egyptian records describe other grain sent to Hatti. And reaching a harbor was only one stage. The Hittite capital stood far inland on a high plateau. After unloading, someone still had to organize animals, carts, labor, and food for the journey uphill. A ship on the coast was not yet dinner in Hattusa.

And there was a third group of mouths that made it worse. For centuries the Hittite kings had fought their wars for people as much as for land. Their own records count the captives along with the cattle: fifteen thousand from one campaign, marched back to the plateau and settled on royal estates to work the fields. That's the Farmer's sister again, and her brothers. So a good share of the people now going hungry in central Turkey had been brought there in chains to grow the food that wasn't growing.

Now watch what the kings do under pressure, because they did something you'll recognize.

Go back now to the later thirteenth century, before those three exceptionally dry years. Assyria was a major rival to the east, with territory taken from the old horse kingdom. The Hittite court was trying to control what could reach it through dependent lands.

So the Hittite king wrote a treaty with one of his subject kings on the Syrian coast, and one clause in it reads like this. No merchant of yours is to go to Assyria. No merchant of Assyria is to enter your land or pass through it.

That's a trade embargo. It's sanctions, around 1230 BCE: you can't beat him in battle, so you try to cut off his business.

There's something else on that tablet that I find hard to look away from. Early in the text there's a list of the kings the Hittite ruler counts as his equals. The king of Egypt. The king of Babylon. The king of Assyria. And then a fourth name was written, the king of the Greeks, and the scribe went back and scratched it out. You can see the erasure.

We don't know why. Maybe the Greeks had just stopped mattering. Maybe someone decided it was an insult to include them. But there it is: one of the powers at the table, crossed off by hand, in the wet clay.

The Greeks, by the way, had been making trouble for the Hittites on the west coast of Turkey for a century. There are letters about it. A lot of the trouble centered on one town up near the straits that the Hittites called Wilusa. The Greeks had another way of saying that name. Keep it in mind until the last part.

And there was trouble at sea.

Third question. Who were the Sea Peoples?

You've probably heard of them, since they're usually cast as the villains of this story: a wave of mysterious invaders who came out of nowhere and burned civilization down. That isn't what the evidence shows, and here's the detail that changed my mind.

Go back to Kadesh. In the pictures Ramses had carved, there are soldiers standing right next to the king with round shields and helmets with horns on them. They're his bodyguard, and they're foreigners. The Egyptians called them Sherden. They'd come raiding the Egyptian coast early in his reign, he'd beaten them, and he'd signed up the survivors.

Fifty years later the Sherden are on the list of sea raiders attacking Egypt.

So these weren't strangers. They were people who'd been on the edges of this world the whole time, as pirates when that paid and as hired soldiers when that paid better. "Sea Peoples" is a label a French scholar made up in the 1800s. The Egyptians never used it. They named separate groups: the Sherden, and half a dozen others. One group they called the Peleset. Those are almost certainly the people the Bible calls Philistines. Goliath's people.

What changed toward the end of the 1200s is that there were more of them, in bigger groups, and they weren't going home. In 1208 the king of Egypt, the one who'd sent grain to the Hittites, fought off an invasion from the western desert. The invaders had sea raiders with them as allies, and they'd brought their wives, their children and their cattle.

People don't bring cattle on a raid. They bring them when they're moving house.

One possibility is that failed harvests helped push some people toward new homes or new ways of making a living. War and political displacement could do that too. A family on the move, a hired soldier, and a raiding crew need not belong to three permanently separate worlds. But the evidence does not identify the motive of every group, or establish the same drought on every island and coast.

A footnote on that Egyptian victory. The king had a monument put up to celebrate, and at the end of it there's a list of places he says he's crushed. One line reads: "Israel is laid waste, his seed is not." It's the first time that name appears anywhere in writing, in 1208 BCE, as a boast by a king who claimed to have wiped them out. Remember that when we get to the hills, two parts from now.

Now the question I most want to ask, and you can ask it about any collapse, including the ones people are afraid of today. Could they have seen it coming?

I don't mean, did they. I mean, was it possible? Was there enough information around that a clear-headed person at one of those courts in 1230 BCE could have stood up and said: this isn't a run of bad luck, this is the end?

I don't think so, and it wasn't because they were stupid.

They saw poor harvests, raiders, late shipments, letters that went unanswered. Those were familiar troubles. The harder question was how much strain the other kingdoms were under at the same time. An urgent letter could tell a court that someone needed grain. It couldn't tell them when all the help they were counting on might fail.

Grain bins and treaties could buy time. That was what made them useful. It could also make the depth of a problem harder to judge: how long could the stores last, and how much could an ally really spare? The letters show alarm, not a world in which everything looked normal.

Let me try a thought experiment, and it's only that. Suppose somebody did see it. Suppose you're an adviser to the Hittite king around 1230 and somehow you've grasped the whole picture. What do you tell him to do?

Store more grain. Grain storage was already part of the state's practice. Buy from abroad. They were doing it. Make peace with your great rival. They'd signed the most famous treaty of the ancient world. Squeeze the new threat without going to war. They'd tried an embargo. Keep the sea lanes open. A later Hittite king would report fighting at sea himself.

Every sensible thing on that list, they did. That's what I find sobering. This wasn't a world that fell because the people running it were fools. They took the reasonable step each time, and each reasonable step leaned on some other part of the arrangement that was also in trouble.

So if we go looking for the person who noticed, we don't find a prophet. We find an accountant.

Picture him. I'm inventing the man, but not his problem. He's the Counter, and he's in a storeroom in the Hittite capital, and the numbers are wrong. He's counted the jars three times this month because he didn't trust the first two counts. The third came out the same. Grain doesn't care how many times you count it. There are fewer full jars than there should be at this time of year, and it was the same last year.

He writes it down. He sends it up. He gets letters back from other storerooms saying the same thing. The provinces are sending less, because they've had poor harvests too. In this imagined storeroom, he's waiting for a shipment from abroad to close the gap.

He can recognize the shortfall. His difficulty is deciding what will fix it, and persuading people elsewhere to provide what the stores need. Knowing that trouble is serious is not the same as having a remedy that still works.

Fourth question. How does bad news travel in a world like this?

It travels the way the goods do. And I think the first people who knew something was deeply wrong weren't kings or clerks. They were the Carrier's people: the ship owners, the caravan men, the agents in foreign ports. To a king, a trade route is a line on a list. To a merchant it's a set of people. The partner in the next port. The customs man at the river crossing. The buyer who takes the wool every autumn.

A king finds out a route has died when the tin doesn't arrive. The merchant found out months earlier, when the partner stopped answering.

I can't prove that from any one document. But there's a letter from these years, found in the house of one of the big merchants of Ugarit, written by one of his agents in a town far inland. I'll paraphrase it. There is famine in your house here, the agent says. We are all going to starve. If you don't get here soon, you won't find one of us alive.

That's the nervous system of the Bronze Age, carrying pain.

And a connected world doesn't come apart by decree. It comes apart when ten thousand sensible people each decide, one at a time, that a trip their fathers made every year isn't worth the risk this year.

Cross the sea to Greece, and you can measure the fear with a tape.

Some Greek palaces had imposing walls. In the last decades of the 1200s they rebuilt them on a different scale. At a palace called Tiryns the new walls were twenty-five feet thick, made of blocks that weigh several tons each, fitted together with no mortar. At Mycenae they extended the wall to take in a hidden staircase, cut down through the rock to an underground spring, so the citadel couldn't be cut off from water. You don't dig that unless you're expecting a siege.

Somebody moved those blocks. That was the Farmer, called up by the palace the way he'd been called up to dig canals in Iraq, and in the season when his own fields needed him. Later Greeks couldn't believe men had built those walls. They said it was the Cyclopes, the one-eyed giants. It was tired farmers and worried officials.

At Pylos, where we watched a clerk at his desk, there aren't any walls like that. But go back to that shelf of damp tablets, in the palace's last year. Among the records of goods and provisions are orders for men and metal.

There's one that orders the officials of every district to hand over bronze. It's specified as temple bronze, and it says what it's for: points for spears and javelins. They're taking metal from the shrines to make weapons. That's the Maker's world under pressure. The palace is calling in metal already on hand. That tells us what it wanted to collect, not whether every shipment of new copper and tin had stopped.

There's a set that lists about eight hundred men, by name of their commander and by stretch of coastline. The heading says, roughly: how the watchers are guarding the coast.

And there's one that lists rowers, about six hundred of them, being called up.

The same administration counts provisions and lookouts. These tasks sit together in its surviving records. Some scholars think lists like these were routine. Read alongside the order for bronze, I think they were written by frightened people.

And then somebody said it out loud.

In the archive at Ugarit there's a letter from the chief minister of the copper island, Cyprus. He writes in the proper diplomatic style, with all the courtesies in the right order. And what he reports is this. Twenty enemy ships were seen off the coast. They've done damage. They've now left, and he doesn't know where they've gone. He's writing, he says, so that Ugarit can be on its guard.

Look at what that letter is. It's the international system, with its scribes and its couriers and its formal greetings, being used to report that the international system no longer controls the sea.

On the Hittite side, the last Great King left an account of fighting at sea. In the surviving text, he says that the ships of Alasiya, the island we identify as Cyprus, met him in battle three times, and that he destroyed them. This was a king from an inland capital fighting around an important source of copper. Keeping sea routes open may have mattered, but the text does not give us a complete explanation of his aims.

He says he won.
