Before the fire I want to pull all the way back for a minute, because none of this was the world.

In these same years, four thousand miles to the east, a queen of China named Fu Hao died. We know her name because it's cast into the bronze vessels in her tomb, and because the king's fortune-tellers wrote questions about her on bones: will Fu Hao's childbirth go well? Should Fu Hao lead the army against the western tribes? She did lead it. She was buried with nearly two thousand objects, and the bronze among them weighs more than a ton and a half.

In China the Bronze Age was at high noon. Nobody there had heard of Egypt or the Hittites, and nothing I'm about to describe touched them. What's ending isn't the Bronze Age. It's one region's version of it, the one that was tied together by ships and letters and brides.

So here's the family in the year 1200.

The Keeper is writing letters marked life or death.

The Counter has added it up three times.

The Carrier hasn't heard from his partner since last summer.

The Maker is being asked to turn the shrines' bronze into weapons.

The Farmer is hauling stone for a wall, and at home there's a jar he isn't supposed to open. His sister is on a ration list, and the rations are short.

Not one of them can help any of the others. Each of them is waiting for one of the other four to fix it.

The tree rings say what's coming next. Three thin ones in a row.


# Part 7 — The Collapse

The last known king of Ugarit was named Ammurapi. Among the letters from these troubled years is one full of good advice.

You know Ugarit from the imagined evening at its harbor. The capital stood a short distance inland from the Syrian coast; its port lay in a nearby bay. Cargo had to move between ship, shore, and city. The royal palace and archives belonged to a prosperous kingdom, but its king answered to the Hittite rulers in what is now Turkey.

By about 1190 BCE its king had been getting orders from his Hittite overlords for years. We have them. Send ships to carry grain. Send your soldiers to serve with our army. There's one where a Hittite official tells him off for not turning up in person, like a boss writing to an employee who's missed a meeting.

He did what he was told. His infantry and his chariots marched north into Turkey. His warships sailed off to patrol the southwest coast of Turkey, three hundred miles away.

Then strange ships were sighted off his own shore. He wrote to the king of Cyprus, the copper island, a ruler he addressed diplomatically as "my father." That title does not tell us the man's age.

One surviving letter from the king of Cyprus offers advice. I'll paraphrase it. If enemy ships have been seen, make yourself strong. Gather your troops, secure your towns, and watch for the enemy. The letters do not come with a complete, securely dated sequence of replies, so we should not pretend we can follow the messengers day by day.

A letter from Ammurapi shows why such advice might be desperately difficult to follow. He reports enemy ships damaging his territory while his own forces are elsewhere.

"My father, the ships of the enemy have come. They have been setting fire to my cities. All of my infantry and chariotry are away in the land of the Hittites. All of my ships are off the coast of Lukka." That's the coast of southwest Turkey. And then: "Seven ships of the enemy have done this harm."

Seven.

Seven ships. The king gives us that number, but no reliable count of the men aboard. He reports attacks on his territory; he does not establish that these were the same crews that finally destroyed the capital. What we can hear plainly is his predicament: the forces he needed at home were serving elsewhere.

Who were the men on those ships? The letter doesn't say. Ugarit's scribes knew the names of the sea raiders of their day, and they didn't use one. So this next bit is me imagining, and I want you to know that it is.

Picture one possible man aboard a raiding ship: someone who once worked a field and can no longer feed his household from it. A boat offers work, escape, or the chance to take food from someone else. That man is imagined. He lets us consider a possible route into raiding, not calculate the odds that a particular attacker had been a farmer.

The families shown in Egyptian battle imagery will give us another reason to think about people on the move. They do not identify the men in Ammurapi's letter. Keep the possibility, and keep the two pieces of evidence separate.

Why didn't help arrive in time? Ugarit's obligations give us one part of an answer: a subordinate kingdom could be required to send troops and ships away. That made this coast vulnerable. It does not prove that every ally was helpless for the same reason, or that every surviving plea went unanswered.

For a long time a story was told about those last letters. It went that they were found in a kiln. The scribes had put them in the oven to bake them hard before sending, and the city fell before anyone took them out. It's a wonderful image, and you'll still find it in books. It isn't true. When archaeologists went back over the dig records, the "kiln" turned out to be a heap of rubble, with tablets in it that had fallen from an upper floor when the building came down.

The surviving tablet is not proof of a message trapped in an oven. A retained copy is one possible explanation for a letter remaining at Ugarit. But finding it there does not tell us whether a messenger arrived, what answer came back, or what help anyone attempted.

We know what happened next from the ground.

Ugarit suffered a violent destruction. Excavators found burned and collapsed buildings, weapons, and buried valuables. Picture what a collapsing upper floor can do to the rooms below: crush furniture, scatter stored objects, and cover an archive in rubble. That is a way to understand the remains, not a recovered account of fighting from one doorway to the next.

The great Late Bronze Age capital was not rebuilt as it had been. Its palaces and archives ceased to function. We cannot turn that into a statement about the fate of every person who had lived there. Centuries of later activity and weather would alter the mound before modern excavation began.

One thing came out of that hill that I asked you to listen for. Among the tablets was a song. It's the hymn to the wife of the moon god, a real surviving piece of music to set beside our imagined doorway singer. It was written down a century or two before the end, and under the words there's a second set of signs, which most scholars read as instructions for the strings of a lyre. It's the oldest written melody in the world. The experts don't agree on how it should sound, and their versions are quite different from each other. But you can go and listen to them tonight. The kingdom ended. One of its songs remained in the clay.

So that's how one city died. Now the first question, which everyone asks. Who did it?

The old answer was the Sea Peoples: one great wave of invaders rolling down the coast, burning every city in a single terrible year. I told you last time why I don't believe in the wave. Here's what the ground says.

The changes unfolded across several decades, and not everywhere at the same pace. Different sites have different histories, and the dates are often less precise than a timeline makes them look.

And it was a patchwork. A few years ago an archaeologist named Jesse Millek reexamined a large body of destruction claims. He checked a hundred and fifty-three published claims of destruction around 1200 BCE against the archaeological evidence. In his assessment, about six in ten did not hold up. Some had been dated wrong by a century. Some had burned in one building and not the rest. Some had no evidence at all, only a line in one book that had been copied into the next.

So some cities burned. Some were emptied without a fight. Some carried on. And the ones that did burn weren't all burned by the same people.

Let me take you to three of them.

The first is Emar, a town on the Euphrates in inland Syria. A river connected it to other places, but it was far from the Mediterranean coast. Its end in the early twelfth century cannot be explained simply by imagining ships beaching beneath its walls.

Before it fell its scribes left us the sound of a city going under, and it isn't screaming. It's paperwork. They kept drawing up contracts in the proper form, with witnesses and seals, and a group of those contracts all start with the same phrase: "in the year of distress."

In these contracts, people sell property or enter another household's service to get through desperate conditions. The terms differ from one document to another. Together they show households running out of choices.

One contract records a couple selling four children, two boys and two girls, including a daughter still nursing. It names the parents and the children. The family explains its desperate need, and the transaction is recorded with witnesses. The people involved have not disappeared into an anonymous number.

The document says the parents pressed their children's feet into clay, leaving impressions to help identify them in the transaction. Not signatures. Little footprints.

Those survive. You can see the toes.

The scribes of Emar had a set phrase for catastrophe because it had become ordinary enough to need one.

The second is the Hittite capital, and it's the one that surprised the archaeologists most.

The evidence does not fit a simple picture of a full palace taken by storm. Important buildings had been largely cleared of valuable contents before they burned. Different parts of the city did not necessarily empty or burn together.

Someone had removed things worth carrying. Imagine the work: loading animals, choosing what to take, leaving other things behind. We don't know exactly when the court left or where it went. The emptied buildings are the clue, not a witnessed last procession.

The central government disappeared from its old capital. The political and cultural world it had helped create did not vanish everywhere with it.

At Carchemish, a city on the Euphrates ruled by a branch of the Hittite royal family, rulers continued to claim that inheritance. The name is worth keeping because it prevents us from confusing the end of the capital with the disappearance of every Hittite successor.

The third is Pylos, in Greece, and you know someone there.

Around the beginning of the twelfth century BCE the palace burned, and nobody rebuilt it. We don't know who set the fire. It might have been raiders from the sea. It might have been the kingdom next door, or the palace's own hungry subjects. It didn't have walls.

Remember the unbaked tablets in the palace archive. The fire hardened many of them. Working records that had not been made as a history book survived because of the building's destruction. The same event that ended the administration preserved much of what we know about its work.

Everything I've told you about Pylos comes from that one fire: the figs, the weaving women, the bronze issued to the smiths. We have the last year's accounts of that kingdom only because the kingdom was destroyed.

And you remember what was in those accounts. Eight hundred men assigned to watch the coast.

Somewhere on that shore was a man on a headland, with a handful of others, looking at the water. We don't know if he saw anything. The tablet says where he was posted. It doesn't say what came.

Other Greek palace centers suffered destruction and major change in these generations. But at Tiryns, the place with the massive walls, the town expanded after the palace burned. People built new houses and continued living there. That doesn't reveal every detail of their leadership or record-keeping. It does show why the death of a palace and the death of a community are different events.

Now turn south to Egypt, where a king left his own very different account of these years.

In 1177 BCE the king of Egypt was Ramses the Third, and he's the one who left the famous description. It's carved on the wall of his temple, and it's the nearest thing we have to an ancient account of the whole collapse.

"The foreign countries made a conspiracy in their islands. All at once the lands were removed and scattered in the fray. No land could stand before their arms."

Then he lists the ones that had fallen: the Hittites, the south coast of Turkey, Cyprus, and others. He says the enemy set up camp in Syria and came on toward Egypt "while the flame was prepared before them."

He met them twice. There was a battle on land, somewhere on the coast road, and a battle on the water, in the mouths of the Nile. He'd lined the banks with archers and let the enemy ships come in close. Both are shown on the temple wall in huge detail. He won both.

Two things about those carvings.

The first is that his list isn't accurate. He names the Hittite cousins' city on the Euphrates among the fallen, and it hadn't fallen. A king's inscription is advertising. When it disagrees with the ground, I go with the ground.

The second is in the picture of the land battle. In among the fighting men there are ox-carts, heavy ones with solid wheels. There are women in the carts, and small children being lifted down out of the way of the fighting.

The carts and children suggest movement involving families, not only fighting men. They do not tell us exactly where each family began, what occupation it had, or why it left. I think of our imagined Farmer and his seed jar. That is one possible human story to place beside the image, not an identification supplied by the carving.

Egyptian royal texts also claim that captives were settled in strongholds and supplied with rations. Exactly where particular groups were placed, and how those claims relate to the later Philistine towns on the southern Levantine coast, is debated. The name Peleset is important to that discussion, but the texts do not give us a simple settlement map.

So Egypt won. Here's what winning looked like twenty years later.

On the west bank of the Nile there was a village where the craftsmen lived who cut and painted the royal tombs. They were skilled men, paid by the state in grain. In about 1157 BCE their grain was eighteen days late. So they put down their tools, walked out past the guard posts and sat down behind one of the temples, and they wouldn't move.

A scribe wrote down what they said. We've come here because we're hungry and thirsty. There's no clothing, no oil, no fish, no vegetables. Write to Pharaoh about it.

It's the first strike in recorded history. They got some of their back pay, and then it happened again, and again. The richest state in the world could no longer reliably pay the men who dug its kings' graves. Within a generation those same villagers were on trial for robbing the tombs their grandfathers had built, and we have their confessions.

And the king who beat the Sea Peoples? There was a plot in his own household. One of his wives wanted her son on the throne. We have the court record of the trial, with the sentences. It doesn't say whether the plot succeeded. In 2012 his mummy was put through a CT scanner. His throat had been cut to the bone.

Egypt survived, with kings, temples, writing, and a great agricultural base. It also lost much of its earlier power abroad and faced serious difficulties at home. The story is of a state under strain, not a country with no one left to trade with.

One more case, far to the east. In the middle of the twelfth century BCE, Elamite rulers from southwestern Iran attacked Babylonia. A succession of campaigns ended the Kassite dynasty that had ruled there for centuries. This was a different political history from an attack on a Mediterranean port.

Elamite kings carried prestigious monuments back to Susa, their center in southwestern Iran. Among the objects taken east were the victory monument of Naram-Sin, the king with the horned helmet, and the great stone inscribed with Hammurabi's laws.

That is why these monuments of Mesopotamian kings were recovered at Susa in Iran. They had acquired a second life as another dynasty's trophies. Both are now in the Louvre; we do not need to put them in one ancient storeroom to understand what their journey means.

So who did it? A single culprit cannot explain these different endings. Some places were attacked. Some ruling institutions withdrew or failed. Environmental pressures mattered, but not in exactly the same way everywhere.

Connections could carry trouble: a force sent away, a shipment delayed, an institution unable to pay its workers. They could also bring help, alternative suppliers, and new opportunities. The evidence we have just followed is a patchwork of destruction, adaptation, and survival. Any explanation has to fit that patchwork.

Now the family, one at a time, because each of them lost something different.

At Ugarit and Pylos the old royal administrations are gone. Elsewhere kings survive, including successors in Egypt and the rulers of Carchemish. The Keeper's kind of work has not disappeared, but the person doing it, and the territory he can command, may have changed.

At a destroyed Greek palace, the Counter has lost the institution that sustained his work. That can interrupt the training of another generation. In Egypt and Mesopotamia, scribal traditions continue. The fate of writing depends on which rooms, patrons, and communities survive.

The Carrier may have lost a customer, a partner, or a familiar destination. Some routes become dangerous or unprofitable; others continue or change. I suspect some people moved between trade and raiding. We cannot give that biography to every captain whose name has vanished from an archive.

A smith whose supplies are interrupted can repair old objects and melt down scrap. Bronze working and exchange do not cease everywhere. A hoard tells us that metal was valuable enough to keep; it does not tell us the owner's exact plan or whether that person survived.

The loss of a palace can also damage the workshops, stables, and provisioning that sustain its chariot forces. Chariots themselves do not disappear from the ancient world. Their history continues under other rulers.

Many farming households survive; others are killed, displaced, or forced to change where and how they live. Losing a collector might mean keeping more grain. Losing a water supply, a market, or protection might mean the opposite. We need to follow particular places before deciding what the collapse did for ordinary people.

And his sister.

This is the third question, and it's the one I can't answer.

Think back to the sister at the grinding stone, and then to the women making cloth for palaces. Not one family followed through the centuries, but different women doing work a household or a kingdom depended on. At Pylos we can see some of them in the ration lists.

What happened to those women when the palace burned?

For most of the particular women represented in those lists, we cannot follow what happened next. The records tell us what an administration needed to record, not everything there was to know about a life. When that administration stops leaving records, our view becomes much poorer.

Maybe some of them walked away free. That's possible. The thing that held them was gone. Maybe some died in the fire. Maybe some were taken by whoever burned the place and sold again somewhere else, into a ledger nobody kept. No document anywhere says.

Some ancient women and dependent people do survive by name. We have just met children named in an Emar contract. What we so rarely recover is their own account of the decisions made about them.

I don't have anything to offer about that except to say it out loud.

By the middle of the twelfth century, the map has changed profoundly. At some ruined palaces the administrative record ends. In other towns people are building, trading, governing, and writing. Their lives do not all fit into the silence of an abandoned archive.

In Greece, memories of powerful kings and great buildings will enter stories passed from one generation to the next. Elsewhere, institutions carry older traditions forward more directly. The next question is what people can rebuild from the resources, skills, and relationships that remain.

Next time, the world afterward. I'd always heard it called a dark age. I'm not sure that's the right word, and I'll tell you why.


# Part 8 — After

Picture a herder below the walls of Tiryns, in southern Greece, around 1000 BCE. We are roughly two centuries after the destruction of its Bronze Age palace. The person is imagined; the massive walls are real.

The wall rises above him in huge, irregular stones fitted together without mortar. Some are as large as a loaded cart. The palace no longer operates as it once did, but people have continued living at Tiryns. A ruined royal center does not mean that every house around it is empty.

Later Greeks would explain walls like these as the work of Cyclopes, one-eyed giants. We cannot date that story to this particular herder's lifetime. But stand beneath the stones for a moment and you can feel the question that invites it: who could organize the work of getting something that heavy up there?

The builders were people, using human labor and organization. What later observers could no longer see was the working arrangement behind the masonry: the food, tools, supervision, and repeated effort. A wall can outlast the community's knowledge of how it was made.

It's Xenophon again, six hundred years early. When the knowledge goes, a story moves in. And archaeologists still call that kind of stonework Cyclopean.

So that's where we are. A hundred and eighty years after the fires, in a Greece that has forgotten its own palaces. I want to ask four questions about this world, and the first is the one that herder raises.

How do you forget how to read?

It seems impossible. Once people can write, how does a whole country stop? But follow the Counter's line at Pylos and you'll see that nothing could be easier. I'm making up the family. The arithmetic is real.

The grandfather is a palace clerk. His script has about ninety syllabic signs, alongside signs for commodities and numbers. The surviving texts are overwhelmingly accounts. He learned a specialized practice supported by the palace, though we cannot reconstruct every detail of how scribes were taught.

In this imagined family, the palace burns while the son is still learning the work. He gets away, but has to make a living in a different way. He remembers signs he no longer uses regularly. No institution pays him to finish his training or teach somebody else.

The grandson is a farmer. He's heard there used to be a palace. He's never seen a tablet, and nobody ever showed him a sign.

That is one way to picture a break in transmission. The evidence shows the disappearance of Linear B administration after the palaces, not the thoughts of this invented family. When Greek alphabetic writing becomes visible centuries later, it uses a different system adopted from elsewhere.

Second question. Why didn't they just rebuild?

The stones were still there. The fields were still there. Plenty of people were alive who remembered how things used to run. Why not put it back?

Because a palace wasn't a building. It was an arrangement between specialists, and each one needed all the others to already be in place. Think of a town with one big factory. The factory closes. The machinists don't open a new factory. They can't. They'd need the suppliers and the customers and the bank and the rail line, and those all left when the factory did.

Rebuilding royal administration means more than repairing a roof. People need workers, supplies, customers, protection, and an authority they are willing or able to support. Some of those connections survive. Others have to be made again. A household can rebuild its own room without being able to reconstruct a kingdom.

So people did the sensible thing. They got smaller.

Archaeologists count the places in Greece where people were living in 1250 BCE, and the places where they were living two centuries later, and the second number is about a quarter of the first. Now, that's a count of sites, and small poor villages are easy to miss. I don't believe three Greeks in four died. Some died, some moved, and many communities were smaller and left fewer possessions in their graves. But the pattern was not the same everywhere.

And yet it wasn't empty, and I want to show you the place that proves it.

On Euboea, an island close to the eastern coast of mainland Greece, excavators at Lefkandi uncovered a very long building dating to around 950 BCE. Timber posts and mud-brick walls once stood above its stone foundations. Inside were exceptional burials. This was substantial construction in a period often imagined as nothing but tiny poor villages.

In one was a man's ashes, wrapped in cloth and placed in a bronze jar. The jar was an antique from Cyprus, already a century old. Next to him lay a woman adorned with gold. Her necklace included a pendant made centuries earlier, probably somewhere in Mesopotamia or Syria. We don't know how it reached her. A little object from a much older world had found a place in her necklace. In the pit beside them were four horses.

Someone here had access to wealth, skilled work, and objects whose histories reached across the sea. We should not turn that into an exact workforce or a complete biography of a chief. The burial and building are enough to interrupt the idea that every connection had gone.

The Keeper's kind of work hasn't disappeared. But authority has changed, and the words leave a trace of it. At Pylos, the title behind the later Greek word basileus belongs to local leaders, including figures associated with groups of bronze workers. It isn't the title of the great palace ruler. That is wanax. After the palace system ends, both words survive: anax appears in Homer as a word for lord, while basileus can designate a king. The words have outlived the old arrangement of offices.

The title changed its range of meaning. That is not proof that every later king descended from a palace foreman, or that the highest surviving official automatically inherited a crown. It gives us a trace of continuity within a changed political world.

Now go back about a century from that burial and travel southeast across the Mediterranean, to Egypt. A text set around 1075 BCE follows an official named Wenamun on a difficult journey. It will put a face, and a grievance, into this world of continuing trade.

In the account, an official of the great temple in southern Egypt is sent on a business trip. His name was Wenamun. His job was to sail to the port of Byblos, on the coast of Lebanon, and buy cedar logs for the sacred boat of the god Amun. We have his report. Scholars argue about whether it's a real report or a story written in the form of one. Either way, somebody who knew that world wrote it.

You've heard of Byblos. Three hundred years earlier its king was the man who wrote to Egypt sixty times, begging for a few archers, calling himself a bird in a trap, throwing himself at Pharaoh's feet seven times and seven times more. Keep that in your head.

Wenamun's trip goes wrong at once. He stops at a harbor on the way, a town now run by one of the peoples who'd come with the sea raiders. One of his own crew steals the money he's carrying and runs. Wenamun goes to the local chief and demands his money back. The chief points out, quite reasonably, that the thief was Wenamun's own man. Nobody helps him.

The account then has him seize silver from people associated with the coastal group called the Tjeker, treating it as compensation for his loss. That matters later. The ships that pursue him are not simply an unexplained second disaster; he has created a dispute of his own.

He gets to Byblos, but taking someone else's silver hasn't solved his problem. The prince of Byblos sends a message down to the harbor: get out of my port. He sends the same message the next day. He sends it every day for twenty-nine days.

Finally Wenamun is let in. He describes the scene. The prince is sitting in an upstairs room with his back to a window, and through the window Wenamun can see the waves of the sea breaking behind the prince's head.

And the prince asks him some questions. Where are your letters of introduction? Where's the ship Egypt gave you for the timber? What have you brought to pay for it?

The prince has records brought out showing what earlier Egyptian rulers supplied in exchange for timber. His argument is sharp: if he and his predecessors had simply been Pharaoh's servants, Pharaoh would not have needed to send payment. He rejects Wenamun's assumption that Egyptian prestige alone entitles him to the wood. The old records show exchange, not an earlier age of free cedar.

That's the prince of Byblos talking to Egypt. Three hundred years after the bird in the trap.

In the end Wenamun has to write home for money. Egypt sends gold, silver, linen, ox hides, rope, sacks of lentils, and baskets of fish. The timber gets cut. And then, just as he's about to leave, eleven Tjeker ships turn up, and their men demand his arrest. He sits down on the beach and cries. The prince, who by this point seems to feel sorry for him, sends down two jars of wine, a sheep, and an Egyptian singing-girl to cheer him up.

He does get away from Byblos, only to be driven to Cyprus, where he has to appeal to a local ruler for protection.

What I like about this account is that commerce keeps working inside the quarrel. There are ships, records, payments, and timber being cut. Egypt's standing is not what Wenamun thinks it should be, but the sea has not emptied and the little port has not forgotten how to keep accounts.

The surviving text breaks off after further trouble, before a completed homecoming. We can leave the missing ending missing. Its value is the world it describes, not a tidy proof that every old power has been replaced by a free merchant.

That prince and his neighbors along the coast are the Carrier's line, and they came through.

Tyre, Sidon, and Byblos were coastal cities in what is now Lebanon. Their people are often grouped under the name Phoenicians. They had rulers, institutions, crafts, and trading networks; they were not towns that had somehow escaped all royal power. Over the following centuries their seafarers expanded their activities westward across the Mediterranean. Political change could create opportunities without making every merchant independent of a king.

The Carrier's work continues under new conditions, sometimes in partnership with rulers and sometimes in private ventures. The contrast is with the vanished palace network, not with government of every kind.

Third question, and it's the one people argue about. Was the dark age dark?

Go to the Farmer, because he's moved. He's in the hills of Canaan now, the spine of high ground that runs down the middle of what's today Israel and the West Bank.

The highlands had a history of settlement before the collapse. Surveys nevertheless show a marked expansion of small communities during the early Iron Age. The terrain made access to fields and water uneven. Springs, captured rainwater, storage, and the labor of working slopes mattered to where a household could live.

They're small. A dozen houses, mostly. The houses are stone, with a few rooms around a yard, and the ground floor is for the animals. There are pits cut in the rock for storing grain and cisterns lined with plaster to catch the winter rain. The hillsides are cut into terraces, which is backbreaking work.

And look at what isn't there. There are no palaces. There are no temples to speak of. There are no rich graves and hardly any imported goods. Everybody's pots are about the same.

Who were they? That's argued. The archaeologist Israel Finkelstein thinks many were herders who settled down when the towns they used to trade with fell apart. Others think they were farmers from the plain who moved uphill to get out from under what was left of the kings. Much of their pottery follows local Canaanite traditions, a clue to continuity rather than proof of where every family came from. And that monument I mentioned from 1208 already has a people called Israel living somewhere in this country. Some of these villagers will become the Israelites of the Bible.

Here is the possibility that makes the idea of a release attractive. In some small communities, households may have had more control over their labor and produce than people attached to a palace estate. But a simple house and ordinary pottery do not prove that nobody collected dues, claimed land, or exercised power. We cannot read a tax exemption from the absence of a palace.

And here's the case against, because I don't want to sell you a fairy tale. More control over your own crop doesn't guarantee food in a bad year, or safety from an armed neighbor. The biblical book of Judges looks back on the time before Israel's kings through stories of raids, massacres, and civil war. It isn't a contemporary report from these villages. Its refrain about a time without a king, when people did what seemed right to them, is part of the book's argument about that past. It isn't meant as praise.

So was it dark? The answer changes with the place and the life we are trying to recover. Some people may have gained room to act while losing security or access to goods. Others faced displacement and violence. I find that uneven picture more convincing than either a universal disaster or a universal liberation.

Down on the coast below him, the other half of that story is settling in.

At a handful of towns on the southern plain, the pottery changes after the collapse. It's painted in the style of the Greek palaces, with birds and spirals. But it's made of local clay. That matters. Imported pots mean trade. Foreign-style pots made locally can suggest people or skills moving, but imitation and exchange have to be considered too.

These communities are associated with the Philistines and the Peleset named in Egyptian accounts. How far Egyptian resettlement shaped their arrival is debated. They brought their own cooking pots and their own kind of hearth. They ate pork, and you can see it in their trash, while up in the hill villages there are almost no pig bones at all. A study of DNA from ten people buried at Ashkelon, one of those coastal towns, adds another clue. Some early Iron Age individuals in that small sample show ancestry linked to southern Europe. In the later people sampled, that distinct signal was no longer detectable in the same way, consistent with mixing into the local population.

In the Bible, the Philistines become some of Israel's great rivals: the people of Goliath, the enemies of David. Archaeology gives us another way to look at those neighbors, through changing settlements, new arrivals, and local continuities. The hill communities and the coastal towns took shape along different paths in the world after the palaces. Their later rivalry doesn't turn those paths into one shared origin story.

Now the Maker, because he's found something to do.

A smith in a disrupted community may have difficulty obtaining familiar supplies. Some bronze production and trade continue, especially in places such as Cyprus. The question is why iron becomes more widely useful alongside them, not how every smith instantly replaces a metal that has disappeared.

On Cyprus, the copper island, the smiths had known about iron for a long time as a curiosity. In the 1100s they start making real tools out of it. The earliest ones are a nice thing to look at: knives with an iron blade, held to the handle by bronze rivets. It's the old metal and the new one in the same object.

Disruption to supplies is one proposed part of the story, but it cannot explain the whole transition. Iron ores are more widely available than tin, while turning them into dependable tools demands fuel, furnaces, skill, and repeated work. Craftspeople in different places solve those problems at different times. A nearby ore deposit helps; it does not make a working iron industry appear by itself.

Early iron was not automatically better than good bronze. Heating iron in contact with charcoal can add carbon; controlled heating and cooling can then produce and harden steel. Simply plunging any piece of hot iron into water does not guarantee a superior blade. This is knowledge built through practice, and its adoption is uneven rather than one invention arriving everywhere in a particular year.

Over time, wider iron production changes the tools a farming household can obtain. That matters enormously. It does not mean bronze had belonged only to kings, or that every village suddenly possessed an independent smith with all the ore and fuel he needed.

That is the answer I can defend: changing supply networks, accumulated technical skill, and the wider usefulness of a different metal. The transition took generations. The name Iron Age makes it sound like a switch being thrown; the objects show people working across the change.

And the Counter. This is the fourth question and the best thing in this part. Where does the alphabet come from?

Remember the early alphabetic signs around Egypt and Sinai, and the idea of using an ox's head for the opening sound of the word for ox. Who first made that leap remains uncertain. I told you to hold onto the ox.

Early alphabetic writing survives in scattered inscriptions over the following centuries. Their small number makes its users hard to reconstruct. It was not simply ignored by every professional scribe: remember Ugarit's alphabet written in wedges on clay, already used before the collapse. Different systems could coexist because they served different languages, traditions, and institutions.

There's one of those scribbles I love. In 2016 archaeologists in Israel found a small ivory comb, the fine-toothed kind you use for lice. In 2022 someone noticed faint letters scratched on its side. If they've been read correctly, and not everyone agrees, it's the oldest full sentence ever found in an alphabet. It says: may this tusk root out the lice of the hair and the beard.

The first sentence we have in the writing system you're using right now is a wish about head lice.

The political disruptions changed the institutions supporting different scripts. In several coastal communities, alphabetic writing continued and developed. A set of roughly twenty-two consonant signs became characteristic of Phoenician writing, carried through trade and other contact. Fewer basic signs can make learning the system easier; useful literacy still requires practice, and it was never automatically shared by every household.

Around 800 BCE the Greeks, who've written nothing for four hundred years, pick it up from Phoenician traders. They keep the letters in the same order and they keep the names, although the names mean nothing in Greek. Alef, the ox, becomes alpha. Bet, the house, becomes beta. They add signs for vowels, which the Phoenicians did without.

So the word alphabet is two Canaanite words: ox, house.

From the Greeks it goes to the Romans, and from the Romans to us. From the Phoenicians it also goes east, to Hebrew and Aramaic and in time to Arabic. Those early experiments belong to the ancestry of many alphabets used today.

For me, the alphabet is one of this story's most consequential inventions. Its early history shows people adapting an existing technology to their own language. Its later success involves traders, rulers, scribes, and communities, not just one profession losing its monopoly in a fire.

Here is a what-if. Suppose more of the palaces had survived. Would alphabetic writing and iron have spread through the same places at the same speed? Perhaps the opportunities would have been different. But both developments had histories before the destruction, so we cannot make catastrophe their necessary inventor. The interesting question is how people used changing conditions, not whether suffering had to happen to give us letters and tools.

One correction before we finish, so I don't leave you with the wrong map.

Not everybody lost the same institutions. Assyria and Babylonia, in what is now Iraq, retained kingship and cuneiform learning through periods of serious disruption and change. Egypt continued its own written traditions. These are different histories from the disappearance of Greek palace administration.

Those differences matter for memory. Some knowledge travels through schools and archives; some through stories, ritual, and practical work. In the last part we will ask what each route preserves, and what it leaves out.

By around 750 BCE, several centuries after the palace destructions, this is no longer simply the first generation making do among ruins. New kingdoms and communities have formed. Trade has expanded in some regions. Greek alphabetic writing is beginning to leave us inscriptions.

Picture a farming household in that changing world. There is still grain to store and grind. Tools have to be repaired, and somebody has to deal with a trader or a person claiming a share of the crop. A mark on a jar may tell us that someone used writing; it cannot tell us that everyone in the house could read or that nobody went to a teacher.

We can recognize our five kinds of work without forcing them all back under one roof. Some are local. Others still reach across long distances. The old palaces have not returned in the same form, but neither has the world become a collection of households that need nothing from anyone else.

That is the world in which stories about earlier kings and their great buildings will be told, retold, and eventually written down.

So what did survive? And how, three thousand years later, did we find out what really happened? That's the last part.


# Part 9 — What Survived

You may know parts of this story. A queen called Helen leaves with a prince of Troy. Greek kings take an army across the sea. Achilles fights, a wooden horse helps bring the war to an end, and the city falls.

But that familiar version combines different ancient works and later retellings. The Iliad, traditionally attributed to Homer, tells a much shorter episode near the end of the war, centered on Achilles's anger. It does not narrate the wooden horse or make him invulnerable except at his heel. Keeping that distinction matters, because we are about to ask what a poem can remember.

Here's where we are. It's about 750 BCE. The fires that ended the palaces are four hundred and fifty years in the past, about as far back from Homer as the first English settlers in America are from us. Greek palace writing had disappeared, and for much of the intervening time we have no surviving evidence of Greek writing. And in those four and a half centuries the Greeks have been telling each other about a great age long ago, when kings lived in halls at Mycenae and at Pylos and wore armor made of bronze.

You've been to Pylos. It's where the clerk sat at his desk by the door, counting figs and wool. In Homer, Pylos is the home of a wise old king named Nestor, who gives long speeches and drinks from a cup decorated with gold, so heavy when full that other men struggle to lift it.

Homer's world includes captives, weaving, household labor, and kings. What it does not give us is the administrative world recovered from the palace tablets: the particular system of officials, allocations, and working records. We should not claim to know everything the poet knew. We can compare what the poems preserve with the quite different things the archives reveal.

And yet he was remembering something, and here's how we can tell.

In the Iliad there's a passage where a warrior is lent a helmet, and the poet stops to describe it. It's a leather cap, he says, covered on the outside with rows of white tusks from wild boars, set closely together, pointing this way and that.

Nobody in Homer's day wore a helmet like that. Nobody had for about five hundred years. But archaeologists have dug them out of graves from the age of the palaces, and they look just the way the poem says.

The helmet is a striking connection between the poem and the material world of the palaces. Oral tradition may have carried the description; surviving old objects or later encounters with them are other possibilities. The resemblance is evidence of a connection, not a recording of twenty generations of singers passing along exactly the same words.

First question, then. Was the Trojan War real?

There's a place. In the northwest corner of Turkey, by the straits that lead to the Black Sea, there's a mound that people have been digging since the 1870s. It was a fortified town for two thousand years, and it was destroyed and rebuilt many times. One of those destructions, by fire, comes at about the right date, a little after 1200 BCE.

That alone wouldn't prove much. But remember the Hittites, the great kingdom in central Turkey whose government walked out of its own capital and vanished. When their archives were finally read, there were letters in them about the far west of their territory. Those letters mention a town up in that corner of Turkey that the Hittites called Wilusa. An early Greek name for Troy was Wilios. They mention a king of that town named Alaksandu. In Homer, the prince who steals the queen has two names, and the other one is Alexandros. And they mention, more than once, trouble in that region with a king from across the sea, from a land the Hittites called Ahhiyawa. Homer's most common name for the Greeks is the Achaeans.

In one of those letters a Hittite king, writing to the king of that land across the sea, says that the two of them once quarreled over Wilusa, and that it's settled now.

Here is what I think the comparison gives us. A real place, political conflict in the surrounding region, and contacts with the Greek world make a historical background for the tradition plausible. They do not verify a ten-year siege, the wooden horse, or the biographies of Homer's heroes. We have found a world in which stories like this could take root, not the war's official paperwork.

I love the shape of that discovery. An archive from a different kingdom helps us investigate the geography and politics behind a Greek tradition. The names are clues to a relationship between history and story, not permission to identify every person in one with a character in the other.

One more thing from Homer's century, and it's my favorite object in this whole series.

By about 750 the Greeks are sailing again. They've adapted a Phoenician alphabet, related to the early experiments we saw around Egypt and Sinai, and added signs for vowels. And they've planted a trading post on an island in the Bay of Naples, eight hundred miles from home.

In a grave on that island, archaeologists found a small clay drinking cup with lines of verse scratched on it. The burial was long described as a boy's, but reexamination of the cremated remains identified several individuals. The inscription on the cup remains one of the earliest examples of Greek alphabetic writing. Its joke matters more here than an unsupported biography of its owner.

The inscription says, in effect: this is Nestor's cup, and a good cup to drink from. Take a drink and Aphrodite, the goddess of love, will have you in her grip.

The joke seems to be this. Nestor's cup in the poem is a heavy vessel decorated with gold, one other men struggle to lift when it's full. Here is a little clay cup announcing a grand name, and promising that a drink will make you fall in love.

Think about where that cup stands in our story. The palace tablets of Pylos belong to a specialized administrative practice. Elsewhere we have already met private letters, poetry, and contracts long before this cup. Writing had never remained only a receipt for barley. The cup shows a different use in early Greek alphabetic writing: verse attached to an object people could handle at a gathering.

After the disappearance of Linear B, Greek alphabetic inscriptions begin to survive centuries later. A smaller set of signs does not make everyone literate in a few weeks. But these early inscriptions show people putting writing to uses far beyond a palace's accounts.

Someone wanted words on a cup to do something to its audience. They were making a joke, invoking a famous name, and playing with a promise of desire. The object gives us a little social moment as well as a place in the history of writing.

Now go east, because I told you not everybody forgot.

Remember Assur, the merchant city on the Tigris where Lamassi lived. The Assyrian kingdom in that northern homeland survived the upheavals around 1200 BCE and later expanded into a great empire. By the seventh century its rulers had made Nineveh one of their most important centers. We have returned to the world whose ruins opened this series.

Around 650 BCE the king of Assyria was a man named Ashurbanipal. He was a conqueror, and a brutal one. He was also a collector. He sent agents to every old city in Iraq with orders to find ancient tablets and copy them or bring them back. Medical texts, star charts, dictionaries, omens, prayers. He boasted that he could read the old dead language of the first cities, and inscriptions, as he put it, "from before the flood."

Among the things his scribes copied was the story of Gilgamesh, the king of Uruk, the one name that got out. By then that story was older to them than King Arthur is to us. And in it there's a chapter about a great flood, and a man who is warned by a god to build a boat and load it with animals.

That collection depended on generations of copying, teaching, collecting, and selection. Mesopotamian scribal traditions survived the disruptions around 1200 BCE; that does not mean one school stayed open unchanged for thousands of years. People and institutions kept doing the work of transmission.

In 612 BCE Nineveh's enemies took the city and burned it. The palace came down on the library. And you know by now what fire does to clay.

About two centuries later, Xenophon and the Greek army passed ruins generally identified with Nineveh. His brief account recorded walls and stories, not an excavation of the city.

Somewhere within those ruins lay tablets from the royal collections, broken and buried, with texts that could illuminate a history his account barely recovered. We cannot put his feet directly above the library or say that he asked questions it would answer line by line. The contrast is strong enough without that invented precision: records had survived where a passing traveler could not read them.

It waited another twenty-two hundred years.

Before I tell you how we got it back, there's one inheritance that never had to be dug up, because people never stopped reading it.

The Hebrew Bible is sacred to a great many people. Here I am asking a historical question: how do its stories, laws, and literary forms relate to older traditions in the Near East? Parallels can show a shared cultural world without giving us a simple route of borrowing for every passage.

You've met the pieces already in this series.

A baby set adrift on a river in a basket sealed with tar, who grows up to lead a nation. We met him as Sargon.

A flood sent to destroy mankind, one man warned to build a boat, the animals, the bird sent out to look for land. We met that in Iraq, a thousand years before the Bible's version was written.

The law that a man who falls into debt and has to sell himself serves for a fixed number of years and then goes free. In the Bible it's six years. On Hammurabi's pillar it's three.

The law about an ox that gores a man to death, and whether the owner knew the ox was dangerous. It's in the Bible, and it's on the pillar, in nearly the same terms.

The Jubilee, when debts are cancelled and land goes back to the families that lost it. That's the kings of Babylon breaking the tablets. The Hebrew term for release is related to an Akkadian term used for release; the institutions and texts are not identical.

And the central idea, the covenant, the solemn agreement between God and the people. It's laid out in a particular order: who is making this agreement, what he has done for you, what he requires, who the witnesses are, and what happens if you break it. That's the layout of a Bronze Age treaty between a great king and a lesser one. We have dozens of them, from the Hittite archives.

Even the poetry has an ancestor. When the burned port of Ugarit was dug up, its tablets turned out to contain hymns in a language very close to Hebrew, with phrases that turn up again in the Psalms.

So the Bible didn't come from nowhere. It's what the old world of law and treaty and story looked like when it was carried forward by a small people in the hills, written in an alphabet with roots in that earlier world of experiments with signs and sounds.

One feature of the Exodus story especially matters to me. It asks its audience to remember enslavement and to identify with people escaping oppression. That does not establish that the surviving text was written by the enslaved people themselves, or that no older work ever spoke from below. It is a powerful use of remembered vulnerability in a tradition carried forward by later generations.

Now. How did we get the rest back?

Second question, and it's the one I'd want answered if I were you. How do we know any of this? How do you read a language that nobody has spoken for two thousand years?

Take Egypt first. The last known dated hieroglyphic inscription was carved at Philae in southern Egypt in 394 CE. That dates a surviving inscription, not the day the last reader died. Knowledge of the script faded over time, while the Egyptian language continued in a later form called Coptic. That surviving language would help make decipherment possible.

In 1799 French soldiers in Napoleon's army were rebuilding an old fort in the Nile Delta and pulled a slab of dark stone out of a wall. It had the same decree carved on it three times, in three scripts. The bottom one was Greek, which scholars could read.

It still took twenty-three years. The man who did it was a Frenchman named Jean-François Champollion, who'd been obsessed with Egypt since he was a boy. He had one advantage. He'd learned Coptic, the language still used in the churches of Egypt, which is the last descendant of what the pharaohs spoke.

Royal names were crucial clues. The Greek text named Ptolemy, and groups of Egyptian signs enclosed in ovals could be compared with that name and others, including Cleopatra on a different monument. Repeated signs helped establish sound values. Names opened a door, but Coptic and the grammar of the language helped scholars go through it.

From those few letters he worked outward. According to a later account, on a September day in 1822 he burst into his brother's office, cried that he'd got it, and collapsed. The story has him recovering for five days.

The wedge writing was harder, because there was no Greek to start from.

The break came from a cliff. In western Iran, on the old road from Babylon up into the mountains, a king of Persia had his victories carved into a rock face three hundred feet above the ground, in about 520 BCE. He had it done in Old Persian, Elamite, and Babylonian, all written in wedge-shaped signs. Then he had the ledge below cut away so nobody could deface it.

In the 1830s a young British army officer named Henry Rawlinson was posted nearby, and he decided to copy it. He copied the Persian text from ladders balanced on a narrow ledge. Later, in 1847, a Kurdish boy reached a harder section using ropes and wooden pegs and took paper impressions under Rawlinson's direction.

One of the three languages was Old Persian, a relative of languages scholars already knew, and it was cracked first, again through kings' names. That gave them the meaning of the whole text. Then, sign by sign, they worked out the version in Babylonian, the language of Hammurabi and the kings' letters.

And a lot of people didn't believe it. The script had hundreds of signs, and the same sign could be read several ways. It looked like guesswork. So in 1857 a learned society in London ran a test. A long inscription of an Assyrian king had just been dug up, and nobody had published it. Copies went to four scholars who claimed they could read the script. Each worked alone and sent his translation back in a sealed envelope.

The envelopes were opened together. They differed in places, but agreed closely enough in substance to show that the method worked.

That test gave strong public support to the decipherment of Akkadian cuneiform. Other scripts and languages needed their own breakthroughs and independent tests. Reading a clay tablet is not one solved puzzle applied unchanged to every civilization.

By then the tablets were arriving. In the 1840s and 50s two men dug into the mounds at Nineveh. One was an Englishman, Austen Henry Layard. The other was his assistant, Hormuzd Rassam, who was born in the town right across the river and deserves to be better known. Between them they found the rooms of Ashurbanipal's library, the tablets lying in heaps where the shelves had burned out from under them. Some thirty thousand pieces went to the British Museum in London.

And there they sat, because there were perhaps a dozen people alive who could read them.

One who taught himself was a young Londoner named George Smith. He'd left school at fourteen to be apprenticed to a firm that engraved banknotes. He spent his lunch hours in the museum looking at the tablets, and he got so good at reading them that the museum hired him to sort the fragments.

In 1872 he was working through a broken tablet and found himself reading about a ship coming to rest on a mountain, and a dove being sent out to look for dry land.

A later account describes Smith becoming so excited that he rushed around the room and began removing his clothes. It is a wonderful story, but we should introduce it as a later recollection rather than a contemporary transcript. What is secure is the discovery that made the excitement understandable: he had recognized a Mesopotamian flood story.

He had found a version of the flood tradition among the tablets recovered from Nineveh. The ruined city in the opening of this series was yielding words again.

Now you're going to read a dead language yourself.

In 1906 German archaeologists began digging at the Hittite capital in central Turkey, the one the court abandoned. They found ten thousand tablets in the first seasons. The script was the familiar wedge writing, so they could identify many signs and approximate sounds without yet understanding the language. Some tablets were in Babylonian, and those they could read. But most were in a language nobody had ever seen.

A Czech scholar named Bedřich Hrozný copied a stack of them in Istanbul just before the First World War. Then he was drafted. He went on working at it in uniform. And in 1915 he was looking at one sentence.

It had a sign in it that every scholar of this script knew, a sign borrowed from the old language of Uruk, and it means bread. So the sentence was about bread. Here's the rest of it, as it sounds.

Bread. Ezzatteni. Watar. Ekutteni.

Ezzatteni. He thought of the German word for eat, essen. Latin, edo. English, eat.

Watar.

In a modern English rendering: you eat bread, and you drink water.

The resemblance was a clue, not the whole proof. Hrozný tested it against more of the language. Hittite belonged to the same broad language family as English, Indo-European, and its texts preserve that family's earliest substantial written record. Across all that time, a word for water still sounds familiar.

That leaves the Greeks, and the clerk at Pylos.

The palace at Pylos was found in 1939. On the first day of digging, the first trench went straight into the archive room, and out came the tablets that the fire had baked. Nobody could read them. Nobody knew what language they were in. Most experts were sure it wasn't Greek.

The breakthrough grew out of several people's work. Two deserve a closer look, and one of them rarely gets the credit.

Alice Kober taught Latin and Greek at a college in Brooklyn, and in the evenings she worked on the script. She refused to guess at the language. She just analyzed the patterns. It was wartime and paper was short, so she cut her index cards from old greeting cards and church circulars, a hundred and eighty thousand of them, and filed them in empty cigarette cartons. From those cards she proved that the words in the tablets changed their endings in regular ways, the way Latin does, and she worked out which signs had to share a consonant. She died in 1950, at forty-three, with the work unfinished.

The man who finished it was an English architect named Michael Ventris. He'd been fascinated by the script since he was fourteen. He developed a grid of relationships between signs, building on work by Kober and others. The grid was not complete before the sounds were known. Patterns suggested possible sound values; testing those values helped him revise the pattern. Then he tried fitting place names from Crete into the grid. And the words that came out, to his own astonishment, were Greek.

He announced it on the radio in July 1952. The tablets, he said, were written in "a difficult and archaic Greek, seeing that it's five hundred years older than Homer, and written in a rather abbreviated form, but Greek nevertheless."

Plenty of scholars didn't believe that either. Then a new tablet came out of the ground at Pylos, one Ventris had never seen. It was a list of pots. Beside each entry the clerk had drawn a little picture. Next to a drawing of a cauldron with three legs were signs that, by Ventris's grid, read ti-ri-po. Tripod. Next to a cup with four handles: four-eared. Next to a cup with none: no-eared.

The tablets recorded an early form of Greek. That changed the history of the language and the interpretation of the palace world. It did not prove that every hero in Homer had existed. The test worked because a proposed reading predicted ordinary words on another tablet: pots, handles, and a vessel with three legs.

Ventris was killed in a car crash four years later. He was thirty-four.

There's a hero in all of those stories that isn't a person. It's mud.

Clay could be an inexpensive, readily available writing material. Under favorable conditions it preserves writing for extraordinary lengths of time. Fire can harden an unbaked tablet, though heat, collapse, water, and later damage can also destroy one. The surviving archives are a remarkable inheritance, not proof that clay makes every message permanent.

Compare this. In 1986, to mark nine hundred years since the Domesday Book, the great survey of England made in 1086, the BBC produced a new one. A million people contributed. It was published on the most advanced medium of the day, the laser disc.

Within fifteen years it was almost unreadable. The discs were fine. The machines that played them had stopped being made, and so had the computers that ran them. It took a rescue team, working with a few surviving players, to get the data out.

The original Domesday Book is nine hundred years old. It's ink on sheepskin. You can go and read it.

Nearly everything our world writes is stored in forms that have to be copied to something new every few years, by a chain of people and machines that mustn't break. That works very well for as long as nothing interrupts it.

The Bronze Age is what an interruption looks like.

So let me try to answer the question I gave you at the start. How do people build a world that connected, live in it for centuries, and then lose it so completely that their descendants stand on the ruins and guess?

Here's what I think the story shows. I've got four things.

The first: connections create capabilities as well as obligations. A household or workshop can obtain things it cannot produce alone. When a route or a partner fails, that can become a vulnerability. Other connections may offer a way through. The question is which relationships survive and what alternatives remain.

The second: recognizing danger is not the same as being able to solve it. The letters show people asking for grain, ships, payment, and help. Stores and alliances could absorb difficulties, but neither guaranteed that the next crisis would be manageable. We should not mistake their failure for proof that nobody noticed.

The third: survival took different forms. A household might rely more heavily on local resources; a port might endure because it kept trading; a state might preserve institutions that another lost. There is no single recipe of self-sufficiency hidden inside all those different outcomes.

And the fourth: memory requires carriers. People teach, copy, tell stories, preserve objects, and give old words new uses. Different carriers keep different things. An account tablet, a poem, and a sacred text are not interchangeable windows into the same past.

Is our world like theirs? In one way, more than I'm comfortable with. You and I depend on strangers on the far side of the planet for things we couldn't make if our lives depended on it, and it doesn't feel like a system to us either.

We also possess something Xenophon did not: ways to bring excavated objects, deciphered texts, and environmental evidence into the same investigation. Earlier people preserved real knowledge as well as stories. Our advantage is not that everyone before us guessed wrong, but that we can compare more kinds of evidence and test more of the guesses.

We read the mail. We can place a run of three exceptionally dry years within a few years of its date. We know what the clerk at Pylos wrote in his last season and what a king of the Hittites said to his gods about a plague. We can bring those different kinds of evidence together. That doesn't give us every answer, but I'd like to believe it counts for something.

I'll finish with the one we can't read.

Far to the east, the Indus civilization built cities with planned streets and elaborate drainage long before Hammurabi's reign. Its people traded with Mesopotamia. Remember the interpreter of Meluhha, known from a seal around the end of the third millennium BCE. The Indus signs survive on seals and other objects, but there is still no generally accepted decipherment.

Nobody can read it. There's no Rosetta Stone for it, no cliff with three languages. Those cities faded around 1900 BCE, and whatever they wrote about themselves is still shut.

So there's a civilization as large as Egypt that we know only from the outside, the way Xenophon knew Nineveh. We know they built those walls, and we don't know one thing they said.

Perhaps another discovery will change that. Perhaps the missing clue was written on something that did not survive. We don't know. The signs are still there, and so is the question of what their makers meant. That is a good place to leave a story about recovering the past: with something real in our hands that we still cannot read.
